Describes correct chest drain insertion technique: Ultrasound guidance, local anaesthesia, blunt dissection through intercostal muscles, finger sweep to confirm pleural space, drain insertion without trocar (APICALLY directed), suture securement, underwater seal bottle connection

Manages post-procedure monitoring: Immediate CXR to confirm position and re-expansion, monitor for air leak (bubbling in bottle), drain swinging with respiration, daily CXR, criteria for drain removal (lung re-expanded, no bubbling 24h)

Recognizes marfanoid features (tall, thin, arachnodactyly, arm span > height, pectus excavatum) and plans appropriate screening for Marfan syndrome (echocardiography for aortic root dilatation, genetics referral)
Counsels patient on pneumothorax recurrence risk (30% after first episode) and indications for definitive surgical management (VATS pleurodesis after second episode or persistent air leak)
Provides appropriate activity restrictions: No flying 6 weeks, SCUBA diving permanently contraindicated (unless bilateral pleurodesis), gradual return to exercise, warning signs of recurrence

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features of spontaneous pneumothorax (sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, reduced chest expansion, hyperresonant percussion, reduced/absent breath sounds on affected side) and differentiate primary (young, tall, thin males) vs secondary (underlying lung disease)

Identify TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX as medical emergency (tracheal deviation AWAY from affected side, mediastinal shift, hypoxia, cardiovascular compromise) requiring immediate needle decompression before chest drain

Interpret chest X-ray findings of pneumothorax (visceral pleural line visible, absence of lung markings peripherally) and assess size (rim measurement at hilum level: <2cm small, >2cm large; or percentage of hemithorax)
Apply BTS guidelines for pneumothorax management: Large (>2cm/50%) or symptomatic pneumothorax requires chest drain insertion; small (<2cm) asymptomatic can be observed with supplemental oxygen

Demonstrate anatomical knowledge of safe triangle for chest drain insertion (apex: axilla, base: 5th ICS, anterior: pectoralis major lateral edge, posterior: latissimus dorsi lateral edge) to avoid damage to vital structures

Describe step-by-step chest drain insertion technique using Seldinger or blunt dissection method: Ultrasound guidance, local anaesthesia, incision over superior rib border (avoid neurovascular bundle below rib), blunt dissection, finger sweep, drain insertion without trocar directed apically, underwater seal connection

Recognize indications for definitive surgical management (VATS pleurodesis + bullectomy): Recurrent ipsilateral pneumothorax, bilateral pneumothoraces, persistent air leak >5-7 days, occupational (pilots, divers)

Counsel on pneumothorax recurrence risk (30% first episode, 50% second, 80% third) and activity restrictions (no flying 6 weeks, SCUBA diving contraindicated, return to exercise gradual over 2-4 weeks)

osces.title: Bronchiectasis Management - Sputum Culture and Airway Clearance
learning_objectives: Assess bronchiectasis severity using clinical and radiological criteria
Interpret sputum culture results and select appropriate antibiotic therapy
Prescribe evidence-based airway clearance techniques
Recognize indications for long-term macrolide therapy in bronchiectasis
Identify criteria for pulmonary rehabilitation referral
Counsel patient on vaccination strategies to prevent exacerbations
Develop individualized bronchiectasis action plan

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Chronic productive cough with increasing sputum volume and purulence over past 10 days

history.hpi: Mrs Chen has known bronchiectasis diagnosed 8 years ago following recurrent pneumonias. She normally produces 30-40mL yellow-green sputum daily. Over the past 10 days, sputum volume has increased to 80-100mL daily, become darker green with blood-streaking, and is associated with increased dyspnoea (mMRC grade 2 worsening to grade 3). She reports increased fatigue and subjective fever but no rigors. She has had 4 exacerbations requiring antibiotics in the past 12 months. Current medications include salbutamol 200mcg PRN, hypertonic saline 7% nebulised twice daily, and she performs daily chest physiotherapy using an oscillating positive expiratory pressure device. No recent travel. Up to date with pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations.
pmhx: Bronchiectasis (diagnosed 2018, bilateral lower lobe predominant on HRCT)

social_history.alcohol: Nil
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband in own home in Young
social_history.occupation_details: Retired 2 years ago, previously exposed to children's respiratory infections

history.family_history: Mother had chronic bronchitis, father deceased (CVA age 75), no family history of immunodeficiency or cystic fibrosis

examination_findings.general: Alert, comfortable at rest, no respiratory distress sitting upright

respiratory.inspection: Symmetrical chest expansion, no accessory muscle use, productive cough during examination with thick green sputum
respiratory.palpation: Chest expansion reduced bilaterally in lower zones, tactile vocal fremitus increased right lower zone
respiratory.percussion: Dull at right base, resonant elsewhere
respiratory.auscultation: Coarse crackles bilateral lower zones (right > left), high-pitched inspiratory squeaks right mid-zone, no wheeze

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, peripheral pulses palpable, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.other: Digital clubbing present, no cyanosis, no lymphadenopathy

sputum_mcs.result_pending: Preliminary: Heavy growth Gram-negative bacilli, culture and sensitivity pending (results available in 48 hours)

previous_sputum_cultures.sensitivities: Sensitive to ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, ceftazidime; resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

chest_xray.findings: Bilateral lower zone bronchiectatic changes (tramline and ring shadows), new patchy consolidation right lower lobe, no significant pleural effusion, heart size normal

hrct_chest.findings: Cylindrical bronchiectasis bilateral lower lobes (right > left), mucus plugging, mild bronchial wall thickening, no significant upper lobe disease, bronchiectasis severity index: 6 points (moderate severity)

spirometry.interpretation: Mild obstructive pattern with incomplete reversibility post-bronchodilator (+8% improvement)

tasks.description: Take a focused history to assess bronchiectasis exacerbation severity and identify potential triggers
Interpret the sputum culture history and chest X-ray findings to guide antibiotic selection
Prescribe appropriate antibiotic therapy for acute exacerbation considering penicillin allergy and previous Pseudomonas colonization
Counsel the patient on airway clearance techniques and assess current physiotherapy regime effectiveness
Discuss long-term management including macrolide prophylaxis indication and follow-up plan

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies key features of bronchiectasis exacerbation (increased sputum volume/purulence, dyspnoea, systemic symptoms)
Asks about sputum characteristics (volume, colour, haemoptysis), fever, chest pain, functional limitation
Reviews medication adherence (hypertonic saline, physiotherapy frequency, salbutamol use)
Correctly interprets previous Pseudomonas colonization as high-risk factor requiring broader spectrum coverage
Recognizes penicillin allergy necessitates alternative antibiotic choice (avoids amoxicillin-clavulanate)
Prescribes appropriate anti-pseudomonal antibiotic (e.g., ciprofloxacin 750mg BD PO for 14 days, PBS code 2933K)
Justifies antibiotic choice based on previous sensitivities and Australian guidelines (eTG Respiratory)
Assesses current airway clearance technique (oscillating PEP device) and frequency (should be twice daily minimum)
Counsels on increasing physiotherapy frequency during exacerbation (to 3-4 times daily)
Discusses positioning for drainage (postural drainage targeting lower lobes) and active cycle of breathing technique
Identifies indication for long-term azithromycin (≥3 exacerbations in past 12 months, current count = 5 including this one)
Explains azithromycin prophylaxis regimen (500mg three times weekly, PBS authority required for >6 weeks, code 11568C)
Discusses risks (hearing loss, QTc prolongation, macrolide resistance) and monitoring (audiometry, ECG baseline)
Arranges follow-up sputum culture sensitivity (to confirm antibiotic choice) and repeat CXR in 6 weeks
Considers pulmonary rehabilitation referral (mMRC grade 3 dyspnoea qualifies for PR)
Documents bronchiectasis action plan (when to increase physiotherapy, when to start antibiotics, when to seek medical review)
Demonstrates empathy and clear communication using lay terminology for complex concepts
Safety-netting: advises patient to return if fever persists >48hrs, haemoptysis worsens, or dyspnoea deteriorates

osces.clinical_context: Bronchiectasis is a chronic suppurative lung disease characterized by permanent bronchial dilatation. In Australia, prevalence is 26.1 per 100,000 adults, with higher rates in Indigenous Australians (147 per 100,000). Management focuses on airway clearance, prompt treatment of exacerbations, and prevention strategies. Long-term macrolide therapy (azithromycin) reduces exacerbation frequency by 31% in patients with ≥3 exacerbations annually but requires PBS authority approval and monitoring for adverse effects. Anti-pseudomonal coverage is critical when this organism has been previously isolated, as Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization is associated with worse outcomes.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess the candidate's ability to integrate microbiological data with clinical presentation. Strong candidates will recognize the significance of previous Pseudomonas colonization and select appropriate anti-pseudomonal therapy despite penicillin allergy. Evaluate understanding of macrolide prophylaxis criteria (≥3 exacerbations per year) and PBS authority requirements. Airway clearance counseling should be practical and individualized. Candidates should demonstrate awareness of bronchiectasis action plans as per TSANZ (Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand) guidelines.

red_flags.flag: Massive haemoptysis (>200mL in 24 hours)
red_flags.action: Immediate hospital admission, interventional radiology consult for bronchial artery embolization, involve thoracic surgery

red_flags.flag: Respiratory failure (SpO2 <90% on room air with hypercapnia)
red_flags.action: Admit to hospital, consider non-invasive ventilation, treat underlying exacerbation aggressively

red_flags.flag: Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection (NTM) on sputum culture
red_flags.action: Respiratory physician referral, consider CT chest, assess treatment criteria per ATS/IDSA guidelines

red_flags.flag: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) - eosinophilia, IgE elevation, new infiltrates
red_flags.action: Aspergillus serology, total IgE, specific IgE to Aspergillus fumigatus, consider oral corticosteroids and itraconazole

differential_diagnosis: Bronchiectasis acute exacerbation (primary diagnosis)
Community-acquired pneumonia (consolidation on CXR, but chronic productive cough and HRCT findings confirm bronchiectasis)
COPD exacerbation (spirometry shows obstruction, but bronchiectasis is predominant pathology)
Tuberculosis (chronic productive cough, but no risk factors, previous negative screening)

osces.title: Interstitial Lung Disease - HRCT Interpretation and Pulmonary Function Tests
learning_objectives: Interpret high-resolution CT chest patterns in interstitial lung disease
Correlate pulmonary function tests with ILD severity and pattern
Differentiate fibrotic from non-fibrotic ILD based on imaging and physiology
Recognize UIP pattern and diagnose idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Assess need for lung biopsy versus confident radiological diagnosis
Discuss antifibrotic therapy indications and PBS criteria
Formulate multidisciplinary team discussion plan for ILD diagnosis

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW (telemed link to tertiary ILD service)
scenario.presenting_complaint: Progressive exertional dyspnoea and dry cough over 18 months

history.hpi: Mr Mitchell reports insidious onset of dyspnoea initially noticed when working on farm (feeding livestock, light fencing work) approximately 18 months ago. Initially attributed to 'getting older' but symptoms have progressively worsened. Now dyspnoeic walking 100 metres on flat ground (mMRC grade 3). Associated with persistent dry cough, worse at night. No haemoptysis, chest pain, or orthopnoea. No fevers or weight loss. Wife noticed 'crackling sound' when breathing. He stopped farming 6 months ago due to breathlessness. Has noticed fingers looking 'different' (clubbing). No Raynaud's phenomenon, no rashes, no dry eyes/mouth, no muscle weakness.
pmhx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (longstanding, on esomeprazole 40mg daily)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (diet-controlled, HbA1c 6.2% 3 months ago)

social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, 30 pack-year history (smoked age 18-48, quit 23 years ago)
social_history.alcohol: Minimal, <1 standard drink per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife on farm property 15km from Young
social_history.occupation_details: Sheep and wheat farmer for 50 years, exposure to agricultural dusts, organic materials, animal feed. No asbestos exposure identified. No known bird/avian exposure beyond farm environment. No occupational chemicals or mining.
social_history.support: Wife primary carer, daughter lives in Canberra

history.family_history: Father died age 68 (myocardial infarction), mother died age 82 (dementia), one brother alive and well (no lung disease), no family history of pulmonary fibrosis or autoimmune disease

examination_findings.general: Elderly male, comfortable at rest, mildly dyspnoeic on minimal exertion (walking to examination couch)

vital_signs.spo2: 94% on room air at rest, desaturates to 88% after 20-metre walk in corridor

respiratory.inspection: Normal chest shape, symmetrical expansion, no intercostal recession, respiratory rate increases with minimal exertion
respiratory.auscultation: Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles (Velcro-like), no wheeze, crackles do not clear with coughing

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual with loud P2 (suggestive of pulmonary hypertension), no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.hands: Marked digital clubbing (all fingers), no cyanosis, no synovitis
examination_findings.other: No rash, no sclerodactyly, no telangiectasia, no heliotrope rash, no Gottron's papules, no lymphadenopathy

hrct_chest.findings: Bilateral basal and subpleural predominant reticulation with honeycombing. Traction bronchiectasis present. Subpleural distribution with relative sparing of upper lobes. No ground-glass opacification. No consolidation or nodules. Pattern consistent with definite usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) per ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT 2018 criteria. No features suggestive of alternative diagnosis (no cysts, no mosaic attenuation, no significant ground-glass).
hrct_chest.conclusion: Definite UIP pattern - idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis most likely diagnosis in appropriate clinical context

pulmonary_function_tests.interpretation: Restrictive ventilatory defect (reduced FVC, normal FEV1/FVC ratio) with severe impairment of gas transfer. Pattern highly consistent with interstitial lung disease.

chest_xray.findings: Bilateral lower zone reticular shadowing, reduced lung volumes, no pleural effusion or pneumothorax

autoimmune_screen.interpretation: No evidence of connective tissue disease

nt_pro_bnp.result: 380 pg/mL (mildly elevated, consistent with possible pulmonary hypertension secondary to ILD)

tasks.description: Interpret the HRCT chest and identify the UIP pattern characteristic of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Correlate pulmonary function tests with ILD severity and explain restrictive physiology to the patient
Formulate a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and explain why lung biopsy is not required
Discuss antifibrotic therapy options (pirfenidone or nintedanib) including PBS criteria and monitoring requirements
Arrange multidisciplinary team review and outline supportive care including pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen assessment

marking_criteria.criterion: Correctly identifies HRCT findings: basal and subpleural reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis
Recognizes HRCT pattern as 'definite UIP' per ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT 2018 criteria (honeycombing is pathognomonic)
States that absence of ground-glass opacification, nodules, and upper lobe predominance excludes alternative diagnoses (HP, NSIP, COP)
Interprets PFTs: restrictive pattern (reduced FVC, normal FEV1/FVC ratio)
Identifies severely reduced TLCO (38% predicted) as key marker of ILD severity and gas exchange impairment
Explains restrictive physiology to patient using lay terms (scarring makes lungs stiff, reduces capacity, impairs oxygen transfer)
Formulates diagnosis: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) based on definite UIP pattern on HRCT plus exclusion of other causes
Explains that lung biopsy is NOT required when HRCT shows definite UIP pattern in absence of alternative causes
States that negative autoimmune screen and serum precipitins exclude CTD-ILD and hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Discusses antifibrotic therapy options: pirfenidone (Esbriet) or nintedanib (Ofev)
Explains PBS criteria for antifibrotics: FVC 50-90% predicted, confirmed IPF diagnosis, no contraindications (requires authority script)
States patient's FVC 65% predicted meets PBS criteria for antifibrotic therapy
Discusses pirfenidone dosing (titrated to 801mg TDS, PBS code 10467F) and side effects (photosensitivity, nausea, LFT monitoring)
Discusses nintedanib dosing (150mg BD, PBS code 10468G) and side effects (diarrhea, LFT monitoring)
Arranges multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion with tertiary ILD service (telemed or case conference)
Refers to pulmonary rehabilitation (mMRC grade 3 qualifies, improves exercise capacity and quality of life in IPF)
Arranges ambulatory oxygen assessment (desaturates to 88% on 6MWT, likely requires supplemental oxygen for exertion)
Discusses prognosis honestly (IPF median survival 3-5 years, but antifibrotics slow progression by ~50%)
Advises pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination (respiratory infections can precipitate acute exacerbations)
Safety-netting: advises patient to report acute worsening dyspnoea (acute exacerbation IPF), new symptoms

osces.clinical_context: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrotic lung disease of unknown cause, predominantly affecting older adults (median age 66 years). In Australia, incidence is 7.5 per 100,000 person-years. Diagnosis requires: (1) exclusion of other known causes of ILD (CTD, drug, environmental), and (2) presence of UIP pattern on HRCT or histopathology. 'Definite UIP' on HRCT (honeycombing with basal/subpleural distribution) is sufficient for IPF diagnosis without biopsy. Antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slows FVC decline by ~50% and is PBS-subsidized for FVC 50-90% predicted. Median survival is 3-5 years untreated, but antifibrotics and supportive care improve outcomes.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's ability to integrate radiological, physiological, and clinical data to diagnose IPF confidently without lung biopsy. Strong candidates will articulate ATS/ERS 2018 IPF diagnostic criteria and explain why this patient meets criteria for 'definite UIP' pattern, obviating need for biopsy. Evaluate understanding of PBS authority requirements for antifibrotics and ability to discuss benefits/risks. Candidates should recognize importance of MDT discussion (gold standard in ILD diagnosis) and arrange comprehensive supportive care (pulmonary rehab, oxygen, vaccinations). Assess communication skills in delivering serious diagnosis with prognostic honesty balanced with hope (antifibrotics available).

red_flags.flag: Acute exacerbation of IPF (rapid worsening dyspnoea, new ground-glass opacities on imaging)
red_flags.action: Hospital admission, high-dose corticosteroids (controversial, limited evidence), supportive care, consider ICU/palliation discussion

red_flags.flag: Severe pulmonary hypertension (mean PAP >35mmHg on echo or RHC)
red_flags.action: Cardiology referral, right heart catheterization, assess for pulmonary vasodilator therapy eligibility

red_flags.flag: Rapid FVC decline (>10% absolute decline in 6 months)
red_flags.action: Urgent respiratory physician review, ensure on antifibrotic therapy, assess for lung transplant candidacy

red_flags.flag: FVC <50% predicted or TLCO <30% predicted
red_flags.action: Consider lung transplant assessment (IPF is leading indication for transplant in Australia), discuss with patient

differential_diagnosis: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (primary diagnosis - definite UIP pattern on HRCT)
Connective tissue disease-related ILD (excluded by negative autoimmune screen, no extrapulmonary features)
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (excluded by negative serum precipitins, no upper/mid-zone nodules, no mosaic attenuation)
Asbestosis (no occupational exposure, UIP pattern can occur but less likely given history)
Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) (excluded by absence of ground-glass, presence of honeycombing)
key_references: Raghu G et al. Diagnosis of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2018; 198(5):e44-e68
Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (eTG complete), Interstitial Lung Disease section
PBS (Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme) authority criteria for pirfenidone and nintedanib, Australian Government
Richeldi L et al. Efficacy and safety of nintedanib in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. N Engl J Med 2014; 370:2071-2082
King TE et al. A phase 3 trial of pirfenidone in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. N Engl J Med 2014; 370:2083-2092

osces.title: Pleural Effusion - Diagnostic Thoracentesis and Light's Criteria
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical and radiological features of pleural effusion
Perform systematic pleural fluid analysis interpretation
Apply Light's criteria to differentiate exudate from transudate
Calculate pleural fluid gradients and interpret diagnostic tests
Formulate differential diagnosis based on pleural fluid characteristics
Determine need for further pleural investigations (cytology, TB culture, pleural biopsy)
Manage pleural effusion according to Australian guidelines

scenario.setting: Emergency Department, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Progressive breathlessness and right-sided chest discomfort over 3 weeks

history.hpi: Mrs Papadopoulos presents with 3-week history of progressively worsening dyspnoea, now breathless at rest (mMRC grade 4). Associated with dull right-sided chest discomfort (non-pleuritic, constant, 4/10 severity), dry cough, and subjective fevers. No haemoptysis. Reports 6kg unintentional weight loss over past 2 months. Decreased appetite. No night sweats. No leg swelling. Denies recent travel, sick contacts, or TB exposure. Has noticed clothes fitting more loosely. Husband states she has been increasingly fatigued over past month.

social_history.alcohol: Social, 1-2 glasses wine with dinner occasionally
social_history.occupation_details: Ran Greek café in Young for 30 years (retired 5 years ago), no occupational exposures to asbestos or chemicals
social_history.support: Husband and two adult children (both living in Sydney)

history.family_history: Mother died age 72 (breast cancer), father died age 80 (stroke), one sister alive (no malignancy), no family history of TB or lung disease

examination_findings.general: Elderly female, appears unwell, dyspnoeic at rest, cachectic (weight loss evident)

respiratory.inspection: Reduced right chest wall movement, no intercostal recession
respiratory.palpation: Reduced chest expansion right side, tactile vocal fremitus absent right lower and mid-zones
respiratory.percussion: Stony dull percussion right lower and mid-zones (up to 4th intercostal space anteriorly), resonant left side
respiratory.auscultation: Absent breath sounds right lower and mid-zones, bronchial breathing at right upper zone, normal vesicular breath sounds left side

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly, no ascites
examination_findings.lymph_nodes: No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable
examination_findings.other: No clubbing, no cyanosis, no skin rashes

chest_xray.findings: Large right-sided pleural effusion occupying approximately 60% of right hemithorax, blunting costophrenic angle, meniscus sign present, mediastinum not shifted (suggests effusion developed gradually), no obvious lung mass visible (obscured by effusion), left lung clear

ultrasound_chest.findings: Large anechoic (simple) pleural effusion right side, maximum depth 8.5cm, no loculations, no pleural thickening identified, no septations, safe window identified for thoracentesis (mid-scapular line, 8th intercostal space)

diagnostic_thoracentesis.procedure_notes: Uncomplicated, patient tolerated well, post-procedure CXR confirmed no pneumothorax

nt_pro_bnp.result: 85 pg/mL (normal, excludes heart failure as cause)

tasks.description: Take focused history to identify cause of pleural effusion (malignancy, infection, cardiac, other)
Apply Light's criteria to pleural fluid results to classify as exudate or transudate
Interpret pleural fluid cell count and differential to narrow differential diagnosis
Formulate differential diagnosis and determine most likely cause based on all available data
Plan further investigations and management including potential pleural biopsy and oncology referral

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies red flag features: unintentional weight loss (6kg), right-sided chest discomfort, progressive dyspnoea
Asks about TB risk factors (born in Greece - moderate TB prevalence country, year of migration)
Asks about smoking history, asbestos exposure, family history of malignancy (mother - breast cancer)
Correctly applies Light's criteria to classify effusion as exudate or transudate
Calculates pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio: 48/68 = 0.71 (>0.5 = exudate)
Calculates pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio: 385/245 = 1.57 (>0.6 = exudate)
States pleural fluid LDH 385 U/L is >2/3 upper limit normal serum LDH (~200 U/L), supporting exudate
Concludes effusion is EXUDATE (meets all 3 Light's criteria)
Interprets lymphocyte-predominant effusion (85%) as suggestive of TB or malignancy (vs neutrophil-predominant = parapneumonic)
Notes glucose 4.2 mmol/L is normal (low glucose <3.3 suggests TB, empyema, rheumatoid, or malignancy)
Notes pH 7.38 is normal (pH <7.2 suggests complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage)

Formulates differential diagnosis: (1) Malignant pleural effusion (most likely given weight loss, lymphocytes), (2) TB pleural effusion, (3) Parapneumonic effusion (less likely - lymphocytes, no fever)
Identifies malignant pleural effusion as most likely based on: age, weight loss, unilateral large effusion, lymphocytes, no TB risk factors
Awaits pleural fluid cytology (sensitivity ~60% for malignancy, may require repeat thoracentesis)
Arranges CT chest with contrast (to identify primary malignancy, pleural nodularity/thickening, mediastinal lymphadenopathy)
Discusses pleural biopsy if cytology negative (thoracoscopy with pleural biopsy - sensitivity ~95% for malignancy)
Refers to respiratory physician for further management (medical thoracoscopy, pleurodesis if malignant)
Discusses potential need for therapeutic thoracentesis or indwelling pleural catheter if recurrent malignant effusion
Arranges oncology referral once tissue diagnosis obtained (for staging and systemic therapy)
Communicates empathetically given likely serious diagnosis, avoids premature definitive statements pending cytology
Safety-netting: advises patient to return if increasing dyspnoea, chest pain, or fever develops

osces.clinical_context: Pleural effusions are classified as transudates (hydrostatic/oncotic pressure imbalance) or exudates (increased capillary permeability or lymphatic obstruction). Light's criteria (1972) differentiate exudates (meet ≥1 criterion): pleural/serum protein >0.5, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit normal. Lymphocyte-predominant exudates suggest TB or malignancy. In Australia, malignant pleural effusion is most common cause of exudative effusion in adults >60 years (lung cancer 35%, breast cancer 25%, mesothelioma 10%). Pleural fluid cytology has 60% sensitivity; medical thoracoscopy with biopsy increases sensitivity to 95%. Management depends on underlying cause and symptom burden.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to pleural fluid analysis. Strong candidates will correctly apply Light's criteria (calculating ratios accurately) and interpret cell differential. Evaluate ability to integrate clinical features (weight loss, age, imaging) with pleural fluid characteristics to prioritize malignancy in differential diagnosis. Candidates should demonstrate understanding of diagnostic pathway: cytology → CT chest → pleural biopsy if cytology negative. Assess communication skills in discussing serious probable diagnosis (malignancy) while maintaining diagnostic uncertainty pending confirmatory tests.

red_flags.flag: Empyema (pH <7.2, glucose <3.3, turbid/purulent fluid, positive Gram stain)
red_flags.action: Urgent chest tube insertion, IV antibiotics, cardiothoracic surgery consult for VATS decortication if loculated

red_flags.flag: Massive pleural effusion with mediastinal shift and haemodynamic compromise
red_flags.action: Urgent therapeutic thoracentesis (remove up to 1500mL initially, monitor for re-expansion pulmonary oedema)

red_flags.flag: Haemothorax (pleural fluid haematocrit >50% of serum haematocrit)
red_flags.action: Chest tube insertion, cardiothoracic surgery consult, investigate cause (trauma, malignancy, anticoagulation)

red_flags.flag: Chylothorax (milky fluid, triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L, lymphocytes >90%)
red_flags.action: Investigate cause (malignancy, lymphoma, thoracic duct injury), low-fat diet, consider thoracic duct ligation if persistent

differential_diagnosis: Malignant pleural effusion - primary lung cancer or metastatic (most likely given age, weight loss, lymphocytic exudate)
Tuberculous pleural effusion (less likely - no TB risk factors, normal glucose, but lymphocytic - await AFB results)
Parapneumonic effusion (less likely - lymphocyte-predominant, no fever, normal pH)
Pulmonary embolism with effusion (less likely - no leg swelling, no pleuritic chest pain, NT-proBNP normal)
key_references: Light RW et al. Pleural effusions: the diagnostic separation of transudates and exudates. Ann Intern Med 1972; 77:507-513
Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (eTG complete), Pleural Effusion section
Hooper C et al. Investigation of a unilateral pleural effusion in adults: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline 2010. Thorax 2010; 65(Suppl 2):ii4-ii17
Porcel JM. Biomarkers in the diagnosis of pleural diseases: a 2018 update. Ther Adv Respir Dis 2018; 12:1753466618808660
Australian Mesothelioma Registry - asbestos exposure assessment for pleural disease

osces.title: Lung Cancer Staging - TNM Classification and Treatment Decision
learning_objectives: Apply TNM 8th edition classification to stage lung cancer accurately
Interpret PET-CT and brain MRI findings for staging
Differentiate small cell from non-small cell lung cancer management
Determine resectability based on stage and performance status
Assess candidacy for curative versus palliative treatment
Discuss multidisciplinary team approach to lung cancer management
Communicate cancer diagnosis and treatment options sensitively

scenario.setting: Respiratory oncology clinic, Young District Hospital (telemed link to tertiary MDT)
scenario.presenting_complaint: Persistent cough, haemoptysis, and weight loss - newly diagnosed lung cancer requiring staging and treatment planning

history.hpi: Mr Norton presented to GP 6 weeks ago with 3-month history of persistent cough and two episodes of haemoptysis (blood-streaked sputum). CXR showed right upper lobe mass. CT chest revealed 4.5cm right upper lobe spiculated mass with ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. CT-guided lung biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma (TTF-1 positive, CK7 positive). Now referred for staging and treatment planning. Reports 8kg weight loss over 3 months, intermittent chest discomfort (dull, right-sided), no dyspnoea at rest but breathless climbing stairs (mMRC grade 2). No bone pain, no headaches, no seizures, no focal neurological symptoms. Performance status ECOG 1 (symptomatic but fully ambulatory).
pmhx: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (metformin 1g BD, HbA1c 7.1% 2 months ago)
Ischaemic heart disease (previous MI 2015, PCI to LAD, on dual antiplatelet until 2016)

social_history.smoking: Current smoker, 50 pack-year history (1 pack/day for 50 years), attempted to quit multiple times, currently smokes 15 cigarettes/day
social_history.alcohol: Previous heavy drinker (8 standard drinks daily), reduced to 2-3 drinks daily over past 5 years
social_history.living_situation: Lives alone (divorced 10 years ago), has supportive adult daughter in Wagga Wagga
social_history.occupation_details: Mechanic for 40 years (retired 2 years ago), asbestos exposure uncertain (worked on brake pads pre-1990s)
social_history.support: Daughter visits weekly, local friend helps with shopping

history.family_history: Father died age 60 (lung cancer, smoker), mother died age 78 (stroke), brother alive age 62 (COPD)

examination_findings.general: Thin elderly male (cachectic), comfortable at rest, no distress
examination_findings.performance_status: ECOG 1 (symptomatic, fully ambulatory, able to carry out light work)

respiratory.inspection: Symmetrical chest expansion, no respiratory distress
respiratory.auscultation: Reduced breath sounds right upper zone, no wheeze, no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly, no masses
examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented, cranial nerves II-XII intact, normal tone/power/reflexes upper and lower limbs, no focal neurological deficit
examination_findings.lymph_nodes: No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy
examination_findings.other: No clubbing, no Horner's syndrome, no superior vena cava obstruction signs

findings.primary_tumour: 4.5cm spiculated mass right upper lobe, abutting pleura but no chest wall invasion identified
findings.lymph_nodes: Enlarged right hilar lymph nodes (largest 2.2cm, FDG-avid on PET), no mediastinal lymphadenopathy
findings.metastases: No liver lesions, no adrenal masses, no bone lesions on CT

findings.primary_tumour: Right upper lobe mass SUVmax 8.5 (highly FDG-avid, consistent with malignancy)
findings.lymph_nodes: Right hilar lymph nodes SUVmax 6.2 (pathological uptake, likely N1 nodal involvement), no mediastinal node uptake (N2/N3 nodes negative)
findings.metastases: No distant metastatic FDG uptake identified (M0)

brain_mri.findings: No intracranial metastases, no leptomeningeal disease, age-appropriate cerebral atrophy

histopathology.immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 positive, CK7 positive, p40 negative (consistent with adenocarcinoma)

molecular_testing.pd_l1_expression: TPS 55% (high PD-L1 expression, eligible for single-agent pembrolizumab)

pulmonary_function_tests.interpretation: Adequate pulmonary reserve for lobectomy (FEV1 >1.5L, TLCO >60% predicted)

echocardiogram.findings: LVEF 52% (mildly reduced), regional wall motion abnormality anteroseptal wall (previous MI territory), no significant valvular disease, PASP 28mmHg (normal)

tasks.description: Apply TNM 8th edition staging to determine stage of lung cancer
Assess resectability based on stage, pulmonary function tests, and cardiac status
Interpret molecular testing and PD-L1 results to guide systemic therapy options
Discuss treatment options (surgery vs chemoradiotherapy vs immunotherapy) with patient in MDT context
Address smoking cessation and supportive care needs

marking_criteria.criterion: Correctly identifies T stage: T2b (tumour 4.5cm = >4cm to ≤5cm)
Correctly identifies N stage: N1 (ipsilateral hilar lymph nodes involved on PET-CT)
Correctly identifies M stage: M0 (no distant metastases - brain MRI, PET-CT negative)
Concludes overall stage: Stage IIB (T2b N1 M0 per AJCC 8th edition TNM)
States that Stage IIB non-small cell lung cancer is potentially curable with multimodality treatment
Assesses resectability: Tumour is anatomically resectable (right upper lobectomy feasible)
Reviews pulmonary function: FEV1 2.35L (78% predicted) and TLCO 68% meet criteria for lobectomy (FEV1 >1.5L, TLCO >60%)
Assesses cardiac risk: Previous MI with LVEF 52%, ECOG 1 - acceptable surgical risk with cardiology optimization
Interprets molecular testing: EGFR/ALK/ROS1 negative - not eligible for targeted therapy
Interprets PD-L1 TPS 55% - high expression, eligible for single-agent pembrolizumab immunotherapy if surgery declined
Discusses surgical option: Right upper lobectomy with hilar lymph node dissection (curative intent)
Explains adjuvant chemotherapy indicated post-surgery for Stage IIB (improves 5-year survival by 5-10%)
Discusses alternative: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy if surgery declined or medically unfit (radical intent)
Mentions immunotherapy option: Pembrolizumab monotherapy possible if high PD-L1 and surgery/chemoRT declined (PBS-funded, code 11653P)
States decision requires multidisciplinary team discussion (thoracic surgeon, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist)
Addresses smoking cessation: Strongly advises immediate cessation, refer to Quitline (13 7848), consider varenicline or NRT (PBS codes available)
Explains benefits of smoking cessation: Reduces peri-operative complications by 50%, improves treatment outcomes, reduces second primary cancer risk
Discusses prognosis: Stage IIB 5-year survival ~50% with surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy (honest but hopeful)
Arranges supportive care: Respiratory nurse support, dietitian (weight loss), social work, palliative care early integration
Communicates diagnosis and staging clearly using lay terms, checks patient understanding
Demonstrates empathy, allows time for questions, involves family (daughter) in discussion if patient consents

osces.clinical_context: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Australia (9,000 deaths/year). Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprises 85% of cases (adenocarcinoma most common subtype). TNM 8th edition staging (AJCC 2017) guides treatment: Stage I-II → surgery ± adjuvant chemotherapy; Stage III → chemoradiotherapy or surgery in selected cases; Stage IV → systemic therapy (chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy). Molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, PD-L1) is mandatory in advanced NSCLC. PD-L1 ≥50% (high expression) predicts response to single-agent pembrolizumab (PBS-funded first-line for Stage IV). Smoking cessation before surgery reduces complications by 50% and improves long-term survival.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic application of TNM staging - strong candidates will correctly identify T2b (4.5cm tumour), N1 (hilar nodes), M0 (no mets), concluding Stage IIB. Evaluate understanding that Stage IIB is potentially curable with surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy. Candidates should integrate physiological data (PFTs, LVEF) to assess surgical fitness and recognize importance of MDT discussion. Assess interpretation of molecular testing (negative EGFR/ALK means no targeted therapy) and PD-L1 (high expression = pembrolizumab option if Stage IV, but surgery preferred for Stage IIB). Strong candidates will address smoking cessation with specific resources (Quitline, PBS medications). Communication skills critical - delivering cancer diagnosis with honesty, empathy, and hope.

red_flags.flag: Superior vena cava obstruction (facial/upper limb swelling, dilated chest wall veins)
red_flags.action: Urgent oncology referral, high-dose dexamethasone, urgent radiotherapy or stenting, tissue diagnosis via bronchoscopy/EBUS

red_flags.flag: Spinal cord compression (back pain, lower limb weakness, urinary retention)
red_flags.action: Emergency MRI spine, high-dose dexamethasone 16mg daily, urgent radiotherapy, neurosurgery consult

red_flags.flag: Symptomatic brain metastases (headache, seizures, focal neurology)
red_flags.action: Urgent brain MRI, dexamethasone, neurosurgery referral for resection if solitary, stereotactic radiotherapy

red_flags.flag: Massive haemoptysis (>200mL in 24 hours)
red_flags.action: Resuscitation, interventional radiology for bronchial artery embolization, thoracic surgery consult

differential_diagnosis: Primary lung adenocarcinoma Stage IIB (confirmed diagnosis - TTF-1 positive, CK7 positive)
Not applicable (histology confirmed, molecular testing complete, staging complete)
key_references: AJCC Cancer Staging Manual, 8th Edition, 2017 - TNM Classification of Lung Cancer
Cancer Council Australia Lung Cancer Guidelines Working Party. Clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of lung cancer. Cancer Council Australia, Sydney, 2020
National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Version 3.2024
PBS (Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme) listing for pembrolizumab (Keytruda) in NSCLC, code 11653P
Quitline Australia 13 7848 - smoking cessation support
Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (eTG complete), Lung Cancer section

osces.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea - CPAP Titration and Compliance Counselling
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and complications of obstructive sleep apnoea
Interpret polysomnography results and apnoea-hypopnoea index
Determine severity of OSA and indications for CPAP therapy
Explain CPAP mechanism of action and titration process
Counsel patient on CPAP adherence strategies and troubleshooting
Recognize cardiovascular and metabolic complications of untreated OSA
Apply PBS criteria for CPAP therapy funding in Australia

scenario.setting: Respiratory/Sleep Medicine clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Severe daytime sleepiness and witnessed apnoeas - referred after diagnostic polysomnography showing severe OSA

history.hpi: Mr Kowalski was referred by GP after wife reported loud snoring and witnessed breathing pauses during sleep (several times per night). He reports severe daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale 16/24), falling asleep during meetings and while watching TV. Denies falling asleep while driving but admits to 'microsleeps' at traffic lights on one occasion (alarming). Unrefreshing sleep despite 7-8 hours in bed. Wakes with dry mouth and headaches most mornings. No witnessed choking or gasping episodes recalled by patient (but wife confirms frequent gasping arousals). Recent work medical required sleep study due to commercial driving license regulations. Polysomnography 2 weeks ago showed severe OSA with AHI 48 events/hour.
pmhx: Hypertension (diagnosed 5 years ago, on amlodipine 10mg and irbesartan 300mg - BP remains suboptimal 145/92)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed 3 years ago, metformin 1g BD, HbA1c 7.8% 2 months ago)

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 4-6 standard drinks per week (mostly weekends)
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife and two teenage children in Young
social_history.occupation_details: Long-haul truck driver (Sydney-Melbourne route) for 25 years, drives 4-5 days per week, concerned about license implications of OSA diagnosis
social_history.support: Wife supportive, concerned about his health and driving safety

history.family_history: Father died age 58 (myocardial infarction), mother alive age 78 (type 2 diabetes, hypertension), brother age 50 (obesity, untreated snoring)

examination_findings.general: Obese middle-aged male, appears tired, no respiratory distress

upper_airway_assessment.mallampati_score: Grade 3 (only base of uvula visible - high risk for OSA)

examination_findings.respiratory: Vesicular breath sounds, no wheeze or crackles
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented, no focal deficit, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 16/24 (severe sleepiness, normal <8)
examination_findings.other: Central obesity (waist circumference 118cm), no pedal edema

polysomnography.position_dependency: AHI supine 65/hour, AHI lateral 28/hour (positional OSA component)
polysomnography.conclusion: Severe obstructive sleep apnoea with significant nocturnal hypoxemia and sleep fragmentation. CPAP therapy indicated.

ecg.findings: Sinus rhythm 78 bpm, normal axis, no ST/T wave changes, LVH suggested by voltage criteria (Sokolow-Lyon)

echocardiogram.findings: LVEF 58% (normal), concentric LVH (LVMI 125 g/m²), grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, no significant valvular disease, PASP 32mmHg (upper limit normal)

tasks.description: Interpret polysomnography results and explain severity of OSA to patient
Explain CPAP therapy mechanism, benefits, and address patient concerns about compliance
Discuss CPAP titration process and expected outcomes with treatment
Counsel on weight loss, sleep hygiene, and adjunctive measures to improve OSA
Address occupational implications (commercial driving license) and follow-up plan

marking_criteria.criterion: Correctly interprets AHI 48 events/hour as severe OSA (AHI ≥30 = severe, 15-30 = moderate, 5-15 = mild)
Explains AHI meaning to patient: 48 breathing pauses/shallow breaths per hour (almost once per minute during sleep)
Identifies significant nocturnal hypoxemia: Lowest SpO2 78%, time <90% for 18% of sleep (increases cardiovascular risk)
Notes severe sleep fragmentation: Arousal index 42/hour (waking up 42 times/hour, explains unrefreshing sleep)
Recognizes positional component: AHI worse supine (65/hr) vs lateral (28/hr) - positional therapy may help adjunctively
Explains CPAP mechanism: Continuous positive airway pressure acts as pneumatic splint, preventing upper airway collapse during sleep
Discusses CPAP benefits: Eliminates apnoeas/hypopnoeas, improves oxygenation, reduces daytime sleepiness, lowers cardiovascular risk
States CPAP may improve BP control (BP currently 148/94 despite dual therapy - OSA contributes to resistant hypertension)
States CPAP may improve glycemic control (HbA1c 7.8% - OSA worsens insulin resistance)
Explains CPAP titration process: Mask fitting session, auto-titrating CPAP trial at home, pressure adjusted based on data download
Discusses expected timeline: 2-4 weeks to adapt to CPAP, improvement in daytime sleepiness within 1 week, BP/HbA1c improvement over 3-6 months
Addresses compliance concerns: Acknowledges CPAP can be challenging initially (claustrophobia, dry mouth, mask discomfort)
Provides adherence strategies: Gradual acclimatization (use during daytime naps first), heated humidification for dry mouth, different mask styles if discomfort
States compliance target: Use CPAP ≥4 hours/night on ≥70% of nights to meet PBS ongoing funding criteria and driving regulations
Discusses weight loss as critical adjunctive therapy: 10% weight loss (12kg) can reduce AHI by 20-30%, may cure mild OSA
Refers to dietitian for structured weight loss program (Medicare CDM plan allows 5 dietitian visits)
Advises sleep hygiene: Regular sleep schedule, avoid alcohol 4 hours before bed (alcohol worsens OSA), elevate head of bed 30 degrees
Discusses positional therapy: Tennis ball sewn into back of pajamas to discourage supine sleep (AHI 65 supine vs 28 lateral)
Addresses commercial driving license implications: Austroads fitness to drive standards require OSA treatment and compliance documentation
Explains need for conditional license: Commercial drivers with severe OSA require annual CPAP compliance report and specialist review
Arranges follow-up: CPAP titration clinic in 1 week, review in 4 weeks (assess compliance, download CPAP data, re-assess Epworth score)
Discusses PBS funding: CPAP device PBS-subsidized if AHI ≥30 (severe OSA), requires specialist prescription and ongoing compliance monitoring
Demonstrates empathy and encourages patient (CPAP highly effective, quality of life improvement significant)
Safety-netting: Advises immediate cessation of driving if falling asleep at wheel, return if CPAP intolerable (alternative therapies exist)

osces.clinical_context: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) affects 9% of Australian adults (higher in obese, male, >50 years). OSA is defined by recurrent upper airway collapse during sleep causing apnoeas/hypopnoeas (AHI ≥5). Severity: Mild AHI 5-15, Moderate 15-30, Severe ≥30. Untreated OSA increases risk of hypertension (2-3x), stroke (3x), myocardial infarction (2x), atrial fibrillation, sudden cardiac death, and motor vehicle accidents (7x). CPAP is first-line therapy for moderate-severe OSA, reducing AHI to <5 in 90% of compliant users. CPAP lowers BP by average 2-3mmHg and improves insulin sensitivity. PBS subsidizes CPAP for AHI ≥30. Commercial drivers with OSA require treatment and compliance documentation per Austroads guidelines.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's ability to interpret polysomnography (AHI, oxygen desaturation, sleep fragmentation) and communicate severity clearly to patient. Strong candidates will explain CPAP mechanism and benefits using lay terms, address realistic compliance challenges, and provide practical adherence strategies (humidification, mask options, gradual acclimatization). Evaluate understanding of cardiovascular/metabolic links (resistant hypertension, poor glycemic control likely worsened by OSA). Candidates must recognize occupational implications (commercial driving requires OSA treatment and compliance documentation) and counsel appropriately. Weight loss counseling is essential - candidates should quantify targets and arrange dietitian referral. Communication skills critical - balance seriousness (cardiovascular risk, driving safety) with reassurance (CPAP highly effective, quality of life improves).

red_flags.flag: Excessive daytime sleepiness with driving (Epworth >16, microsleeps while driving)
red_flags.action: Advise immediate cessation of commercial driving until OSA treated and controlled, notify GP for fitness to drive assessment, urgent CPAP initiation

red_flags.flag: Severe nocturnal hypoxemia (SpO2 <80% for >10% of sleep time) with pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction
red_flags.action: Consider nocturnal oxygen supplementation in addition to CPAP, cardiology referral, echocardiogram to assess RV function and pulmonary pressures

red_flags.flag: Central sleep apnoea predominant (>50% of events central) or Cheyne-Stokes respiration
red_flags.action: Cardiac assessment for heart failure (LVEF, BNP), consider adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) instead of CPAP, cardiology referral

red_flags.flag: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (BMI >30 with daytime hypercapnia PaCO2 >45mmHg)
red_flags.action: Arterial blood gas, consider bilevel PAP (BiPAP) instead of CPAP, urgent respiratory physician referral

differential_diagnosis: Obstructive sleep apnoea (confirmed diagnosis - polysomnography AHI 48/hour)
Not applicable (polysomnography diagnostic)
key_references: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (eTG complete), Obstructive Sleep Apnoea section
Australasian Sleep Association (ASA) Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Apnoea 2022
Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022: Commercial Vehicle Driver medical standards for sleep disorders
PBS (Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme) authority criteria for CPAP device subsidy
Epstein LJ et al. Clinical guideline for the evaluation, management and long-term care of obstructive sleep apnea in adults. J Clin Sleep Med 2009; 5(3):263-276

osces.title: Tuberculosis - IGRA Testing and Directly Observed Therapy Initiation
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical and radiological features of pulmonary tuberculosis
Interpret tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay results
Differentiate active TB from latent TB infection
Prescribe appropriate anti-tuberculosis therapy regimen
Explain directly observed therapy (DOT) requirements in Australia
Recognize notification requirements for TB in NSW
Counsel on infection control and contact tracing

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW (TB service consultation)

patient_demographics.name: Thuy Nguyen
patient_demographics.cultural_background: Vietnamese-Australian (migrated to Australia 2018 from Ho Chi Minh City)

scenario.presenting_complaint: Persistent cough, night sweats, and weight loss - CXR showing right upper lobe infiltrate suspicious for tuberculosis

history.hpi: Ms Nguyen presents with 8-week history of productive cough (initially dry, now producing small amounts of yellow sputum, occasional blood-streaking), drenching night sweats (requiring pajama changes 3-4 times per week), and 7kg unintentional weight loss. Also reports low-grade fevers (subjective, no thermometer readings), fatigue, and decreased appetite. No dyspnoea at rest. No chest pain. GP ordered CXR 1 week ago showing right upper lobe infiltrate with cavitation, suspicious for tuberculosis. Three sputum samples collected (AFB smears pending). Patient has history of BCG vaccination in childhood (Vietnam). No known TB contacts in Australia, but visited family in Ho Chi Minh City 10 months ago (stayed 6 weeks). Family history: Uncle in Vietnam diagnosed with TB in 2015, treated successfully.
pmhx: BCG vaccination (childhood, visible scar left upper arm)
medications: Nil regular medications
Has been taking paracetamol 1g QID for fever (self-prescribed)

social_history.alcohol: Nil
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband and 2 young children (ages 3 and 5 years) in 2-bedroom unit in Young
social_history.occupation_details: Works as chef in Vietnamese restaurant (5 days/week, handles food preparation), has continued working until last week
social_history.support: Husband supportive, extended family in Vietnam

history.family_history: Uncle had pulmonary TB 2015 (Vietnam, treated successfully), father has diabetes, mother hypertensive, children healthy

examination_findings.general: Thin young female, appears unwell, comfortable at rest

respiratory.auscultation: Reduced breath sounds right upper zone, scattered coarse crackles right upper zone, no wheeze

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.lymph_nodes: No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy
examination_findings.other: BCG scar left upper arm, no clubbing, no cyanosis, no rash

chest_xray.findings: Right upper lobe heterogeneous opacity with areas of cavitation (largest cavity ~2cm diameter), patchy infiltrates right upper lobe, no pleural effusion, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy visible on plain film, left lung clear

ct_chest.findings: Right upper lobe consolidation with central cavitation (2.3cm cavity), tree-in-bud opacities right upper lobe (bronchogenic spread), small centrilobular nodules bilateral upper lobes, right hilar lymphadenopathy (nodes up to 1.5cm), no pleural effusion. Appearances highly suggestive of active pulmonary tuberculosis.

sputum_afb_smears.date: 1 week ago (3 early morning samples collected by GP)
sputum_afb_smears.specimen_1: AFB 2+ (moderate number of acid-fast bacilli seen - indicates high bacterial load)
sputum_afb_smears.culture: Pending (Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture requires 4-6 weeks), gene Xpert MTB/RIF ordered (rapid PCR test)
sputum_afb_smears.interpretation: Multiple positive AFB smears - presumptive diagnosis active pulmonary tuberculosis, patient highly infectious

genexpert_mtb_rif.result: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DETECTED, Rifampicin resistance NOT DETECTED
genexpert_mtb_rif.interpretation: Confirms Mycobacterium tuberculosis, sensitive to rifampicin (suggests drug-sensitive TB, but full sensitivities pending culture)

interferon_gamma_release_assay.result: POSITIVE (TB antigen response 5.8 IU/mL, cut-off >0.35 IU/mL)
interferon_gamma_release_assay.interpretation: Indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (cannot differentiate active from latent TB, clinical/radiological correlation required)

tuberculin_skin_test.date: Not performed (IGRA preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals, TST has false-positive risk)

hiv_serology.date: 1 week ago (routine in all TB cases)

liver_function_tests.interpretation: Normal baseline liver function (important - anti-TB drugs are hepatotoxic)

visual_acuity.color_vision: Normal Ishihara plates (important - ethambutol can cause optic neuritis)

tasks.description: Interpret investigation results to confirm diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis
Prescribe appropriate first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy (RIPE regimen)
Explain directly observed therapy (DOT) requirements and rationale for intensive phase monitoring
Counsel on infection control measures and arrange respiratory isolation/contact tracing
Discuss notification requirements, monitoring for drug toxicity, and treatment duration

marking_criteria.criterion: Confirms diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis based on: Clinical features (cough, night sweats, weight loss) + CXR/CT (cavitation, tree-in-bud) + AFB smears positive + GeneXpert MTB/RIF positive
Recognizes AFB 2+ on sputum smears indicates high bacterial load and patient is highly infectious (respiratory isolation required)
Interprets GeneXpert result: MTB detected, rifampicin resistance NOT detected (drug-sensitive TB likely, start standard RIPE regimen)
Explains IGRA positive confirms TB infection but cannot differentiate active from latent (requires clinical/radiological correlation)
Prescribes first-line anti-TB therapy (RIPE regimen): Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol

Specifies correct dosing for 48kg patient (weight-based dosing critical): Rifampicin 450mg daily (10mg/kg, max 600mg), Isoniazid 300mg daily (5mg/kg, max 300mg), Pyrazinamide 1000mg daily (~25mg/kg, 20-30mg/kg range), Ethambutol 800mg daily (~15mg/kg, 15-20mg/kg range)
States intensive phase duration: 2 months (RIPE all 4 drugs), followed by continuation phase 4 months (RI only)
Prescribes pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 25mg daily with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy
Explains directly observed therapy (DOT) requirement: TB nurse/healthcare worker observes patient swallow medications 5 days/week during intensive phase
Justifies DOT: Ensures adherence, prevents drug resistance, monitors for side effects, early detection of treatment failure
Arranges respiratory isolation until sputum smears negative (usually 2 weeks of treatment, requires 3 consecutive negative AFB smears)
Advises patient to avoid public places, wear mask if must leave isolation, cover mouth when coughing (respiratory droplet precautions)
Initiates contact tracing: Household contacts (husband, 2 children ages 3 and 5), workplace contacts (restaurant staff), TB service coordinates
Explains children <5 years are high-risk contacts - require urgent IGRA testing and clinical assessment (may require prophylactic isoniazid if exposed)
States TB is notifiable disease in NSW - Public Health Unit notification mandatory within 5 days of diagnosis (doctor's responsibility)
Arranges baseline monitoring: LFTs, FBC, creatinine, visual acuity (already done), uric acid (pyrazinamide can cause gout)
Plans monitoring schedule: LFTs fortnightly for first 2 months (hepatotoxicity risk - rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide), monthly visual acuity (ethambutol optic neuritis)

Counsels on drug side effects: Hepatotoxicity (nausea, jaundice, abdominal pain → stop drugs immediately, urgent LFTs), orange urine/tears (rifampicin - harmless but warn about contact lens staining), visual changes (ethambutol → urgent ophthalmology)
Advises patient to avoid alcohol during treatment (increases hepatotoxicity risk)
Discusses total treatment duration: 6 months if drug-sensitive TB with clinical response (2 months RIPE, 4 months RI)
Arranges follow-up: Weekly during intensive phase (DOT + clinical assessment), monthly during continuation phase, repeat CXR at 2 months and end of treatment
Communicates empathetically, addresses cultural considerations (language barriers, stigma in some communities), reassures TB is curable with adherence
Safety-netting: Advises patient to seek immediate medical attention if: Severe nausea/vomiting, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain (hepatotoxicity), visual changes (optic neuritis), rash

osces.clinical_context: Tuberculosis remains a significant public health issue in Australia, with 1,300 notifications annually (incidence 5.3 per 100,000). Over 90% of cases occur in overseas-born individuals from high-TB-burden countries (South-East Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Western Pacific). Active pulmonary TB diagnosis requires: clinical features + CXR abnormalities + microbiological confirmation (AFB smears, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, culture). GeneXpert provides result within 2 hours and detects rifampicin resistance (marker for MDR-TB). Standard treatment for drug-sensitive TB is RIPE regimen: 2 months intensive phase (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) + 4 months continuation phase (Rifampicin, Isoniazid). Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is recommended in Australia to ensure adherence and prevent drug resistance. TB is notifiable in all Australian states. Contact tracing focuses on household and close contacts, especially children <5 years and immunocompromised individuals.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to TB diagnosis (integrating clinical, radiological, and microbiological data). Strong candidates will correctly prescribe weight-based dosing of RIPE regimen and add pyridoxine for neuropathy prevention. Evaluate understanding of DOT rationale (adherence, resistance prevention) and implementation. Candidates must recognize respiratory isolation requirements (AFB-positive sputum) and high-priority contact tracing (children <5 years). Assess knowledge of notification requirements (mandatory reporting to Public Health Unit within 5 days in NSW). Strong candidates will outline comprehensive monitoring schedule (LFTs fortnightly, visual acuity monthly) and counsel on serious side effects (hepatotoxicity, optic neuritis). Communication skills critical - addressing stigma, language barriers, and emphasizing curability with adherence.

red_flags.flag: Drug-induced hepatotoxicity (ALT >3x ULN with symptoms or >5x ULN asymptomatic)
red_flags.action: STOP all anti-TB drugs immediately, urgent hepatology consult, reintroduce drugs sequentially after LFTs normalize (challenge testing to identify culprit)

red_flags.flag: Ethambutol-induced optic neuritis (decreased visual acuity, red-green color blindness, central scotoma)
red_flags.action: STOP ethambutol immediately, urgent ophthalmology referral, may be irreversible if continued

red_flags.flag: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB: resistant to rifampicin AND isoniazid) detected on GeneXpert or culture
red_flags.action: Isolate patient (negative pressure room if possible), infectious diseases specialist referral, second-line TB drugs (moxifloxacin, linezolid, bedaquiline, etc.), treatment duration 18-24 months

red_flags.flag: TB meningitis or miliary TB (disseminated TB)
red_flags.action: Hospital admission, add corticosteroids (dexamethasone), extend treatment to 12 months, neuroimaging, lumbar puncture

red_flags.flag: Pregnancy during TB treatment
red_flags.action: Continue treatment (untreated TB worse risk than drugs), AVOID pyrazinamide in first trimester if possible, rifampicin reduces OCP efficacy (barrier contraception), pyridoxine dose increase to 50mg daily

differential_diagnosis: Active pulmonary tuberculosis (confirmed diagnosis - AFB-positive sputum, GeneXpert MTB positive, cavitary CXR)
Not applicable (diagnosis confirmed)
key_references: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (eTG complete), Tuberculosis section
NSW Health Tuberculosis Guidelines 2022
Australian Mycobacterium Reference Laboratory (AMRL) - GeneXpert interpretation guidelines
WHO Treatment Guidelines for Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis and Patient Care (2017 update)

Nahid P et al. Official American Thoracic Society/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis. Clin Infect Dis 2016; 63(7):e147-e195
PBS Authority prescriptions for anti-tuberculosis medications (S100 program)

osces.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome - Berlin Criteria and Ventilation Strategy
learning_objectives: Apply Berlin criteria to diagnose and classify ARDS severity
Recognize precipitants and pathophysiology of ARDS
Prescribe evidence-based mechanical ventilation strategy (lung-protective ventilation)
Calculate PaO2/FiO2 ratio and interpret severity
Manage fluid balance and supportive care in ARDS
Recognize indications for prone positioning and ECMO
Identify complications of mechanical ventilation

scenario.setting: Intensive Care Unit, Young District Hospital, NSW (retrieval team en route from tertiary ICU)
scenario.presenting_complaint: Severe hypoxemic respiratory failure secondary to bilateral pneumonia - intubated and ventilated 6 hours ago

history.hpi: Mr O'Brien presented to ED 8 hours ago with 4-day history of progressive dyspnoea, productive cough (purulent sputum), fever (39.2°C at home), and rigors. Initially managed with supplemental oxygen via Hudson mask (FiO2 0.6) but developed worsening hypoxemia (SpO2 85%) and respiratory distress despite maximal oxygen therapy. CXR showed bilateral infiltrates. Intubated 6 hours ago for severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. Current ventilator settings: Assist-Control mode, TV 500mL (8mL/kg IBW), RR 20, PEEP 8 cmH2O, FiO2 0.8. Latest ABG shows PaO2 68mmHg on FiO2 0.8 (PaO2/FiO2 ratio 85 - severe ARDS). No improvement with recruitment maneuvers. Background: Previously well apart from hypertension. Non-smoker. Lives on farm with wife.

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 2-3 standard drinks per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife on farm property near Young
social_history.occupation_details: Sheep farmer, no occupational lung exposures identified

examination_findings.general: Intubated and mechanically ventilated, sedated (RASS -3), appears critically unwell

vital_signs.bp: 92/58 mmHg (MAP 69 mmHg - borderline, on 500mL fluid bolus)
vital_signs.spo2: 89% on FiO2 0.8 (severe hypoxemia despite high FiO2)

respiratory.inspection: Intubated (oral ETT 8.0mm, secured 22cm at lips), bilateral chest rise symmetrical but reduced, no pneumothorax clinically
respiratory.auscultation: Coarse crackles bilateral lung fields, equal air entry (bronchial breath sounds both sides)

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, MAP 69mmHg (adequate for perfusion but borderline), JVP not visible (flat - suggests hypovolemia), peripheral pulses present, cool peripheries (poor perfusion), capillary refill 3 seconds
examination_findings.other: Sedated, pupils equal and reactive, no rash, no peripheral edema, urinary catheter draining concentrated urine (oliguria - 20mL/hr last hour)

chest_xray.findings: Bilateral diffuse airspace opacification (ground-glass and consolidation), no significant pleural effusions, ETT 3cm above carina (good position), no pneumothorax, cardiac size normal, consistent with ARDS

ct_chest.date: Not yet performed (patient too unstable for transfer to CT scanner)
ct_chest.planned: Once stabilized - to assess for complications (pneumothorax, barotrauma) and rule out alternative diagnoses

renal_function.creatinine: 135 μmol/L (elevated from baseline 88 μmol/L - acute kidney injury)

sputum_culture.result_pending: Preliminary Gram stain: Gram-positive diplococci (Streptococcus pneumoniae suspected), culture pending

echocardiogram.findings: LVEF 55% (normal), no regional wall motion abnormalities, no significant valvular disease, IVC dilated (fluid overloaded), estimated PASP 38mmHg (mildly elevated)

tasks.description: Apply Berlin criteria to diagnose ARDS and classify severity
Adjust ventilator settings to lung-protective ventilation strategy (low tidal volume, appropriate PEEP)
Manage fluid balance and hemodynamic support in ARDS
Discuss adjunctive therapies (prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade) and escalation (ECMO)
Address infection source control and supportive care

marking_criteria.criterion: Applies Berlin criteria to diagnose ARDS: (1) Acute onset <1 week, (2) Bilateral opacities on CXR, (3) Not fully explained by cardiac failure (echo shows normal LVEF), (4) Hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 <300mmHg)
Calculates PaO2/FiO2 ratio correctly: 68mmHg / 0.8 = 85 mmHg
Classifies as SEVERE ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <100mmHg on PEEP ≥5 cmH2O per Berlin criteria)
Identifies precipitant: Severe bilateral pneumonia (likely Streptococcus pneumoniae based on Gram stain)
Recognizes current tidal volume 8mL/kg IBW is TOO HIGH - lung-protective ventilation requires 6mL/kg IBW (ARDSNet protocol)
Calculates correct tidal volume: IBW 62.5kg × 6mL/kg = 375mL (reduce from 500mL to 375mL)
Increases PEEP from 8 to 12-14 cmH2O (higher PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli, improves oxygenation in severe ARDS)
Maintains plateau pressure <30 cmH2O (current 32 cmH2O - reducing tidal volume will lower plateau pressure, prevents barotrauma)
Accepts permissive hypercapnia (PaCO2 48mmHg acceptable if pH >7.20) - prioritize lung protection over normocapnia
Discusses fluid management: Currently positive 2320mL in 6 hours - conservative fluid strategy reduces ARDS duration (FACTT trial)
Recommends cautious fluid resuscitation: Maintain MAP >65mmHg with vasopressors (noradrenaline) rather than excessive fluids
Addresses oliguria: Urine output 20mL/hr (oliguria) - likely pre-renal AKI from hypoperfusion, BUT avoid fluid overload (worsens ARDS)
Recommends prone positioning (16 hours daily) for severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150mmHg) - improves survival by 50% (PROSEVA trial)
Discusses neuromuscular blockade (cisatracurium infusion) for first 48 hours if PaO2/FiO2 <150mmHg - reduces ventilator dyssynchrony, improves oxygenation
States NO ROLE for corticosteroids in early ARDS secondary to pneumonia (may increase mortality per DEXA-ARDS trial)
Recognizes indications for ECMO referral: Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <80mmHg) refractory to optimized ventilation and prone positioning
Contacts tertiary ICU retrieval team for ECMO consideration (patient has PaO2/FiO2 85, already meets ECMO criteria if no improvement)
Continues appropriate antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin for severe CAP (covers Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypicals)
Addresses source control: Pneumonia is source - no surgical intervention required, optimize antibiotics
Implements VTE prophylaxis (LMWH or mechanical prophylaxis if contraindicated)
Implements stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI IV)
Plans daily sedation interruption/lightening (reduces ICU length of stay, improves outcomes)
Communicates with family: Explains ARDS diagnosis, severity, treatment plan, guarded prognosis (severe ARDS mortality ~40%)

osces.clinical_context: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a severe inflammatory lung injury characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, pulmonary edema, and hypoxemic respiratory failure. Berlin criteria (2012) define ARDS by timing (<1 week), bilateral CXR opacities, PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300mmHg on PEEP ≥5, and absence of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Severity: Mild (200-300), Moderate (100-200), Severe (<100). Mortality: Mild 27%, Moderate 32%, Severe 45%. Lung-protective ventilation (ARDSNet protocol) is cornerstone: tidal volume 6mL/kg IBW, plateau pressure <30cmH2O. Adjuncts for severe ARDS: prone positioning 16hrs/day (PROSEVA trial: 50% mortality reduction), neuromuscular blockade first 48hrs (ACURASYS trial), conservative fluid strategy (FACTT trial). ECMO reserved for refractory severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <80mmHg despite optimization).
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic application of Berlin criteria and ARDS severity classification. Strong candidates will identify current ventilation as NON-protective (TV 8mL/kg, needs reduction to 6mL/kg) and adjust settings appropriately (reduce TV to 375mL, increase PEEP to 12-14cmH2O, accept permissive hypercapnia). Evaluate understanding of conservative fluid strategy (avoid excessive fluids despite oliguria, use vasopressors for MAP target). Candidates should recognize severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 85) mandates prone positioning and consideration of neuromuscular blockade. Strong candidates will identify ECMO referral criteria met and contact retrieval team. Assess ability to balance competing priorities (lung protection vs adequate oxygenation, fluid resuscitation vs ARDS worsening). Communication skills critical - explaining complex critical illness to family with realistic prognostication.

red_flags.flag: Pneumothorax during mechanical ventilation (sudden desaturation, unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension)
red_flags.action: URGENT needle decompression (2nd ICS midclavicular line), followed by chest tube insertion, reduce PEEP if possible

red_flags.flag: Refractory hypoxemia (PaO2 <60mmHg despite FiO2 1.0, PEEP 15, prone positioning)
red_flags.action: URGENT ECMO referral, contact tertiary ICU retrieval team, consider inhaled nitric oxide as bridge

red_flags.flag: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) - new infiltrate, purulent secretions, fever after 48 hours ventilation
red_flags.action: Bronchoscopy with BAL, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem + vancomycin), de-escalate based on cultures

red_flags.flag: Auto-PEEP/breath-stacking (dynamic hyperinflation causing hypotension)
red_flags.action: Disconnect ventilator briefly to allow exhalation, reduce respiratory rate, increase expiratory time, consider sedation/paralysis

differential_diagnosis: ARDS secondary to severe bilateral pneumonia (confirmed diagnosis - Berlin criteria met, PaO2/FiO2 85)
Not applicable (ARDS diagnosis confirmed)
key_references: ARDS Definition Task Force. Acute respiratory distress syndrome: the Berlin Definition. JAMA 2012; 307(23):2526-2533
ARDSNet (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network). Ventilation with lower tidal volumes as compared with traditional tidal volumes for acute lung injury and ARDS. N Engl J Med 2000; 342:1301-1308
Guérin C et al. Prone positioning in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSEVA trial). N Engl J Med 2013; 368:2159-2168
Papazian L et al. Neuromuscular blockers in early acute respiratory distress syndrome (ACURASYS trial). N Engl J Med 2010; 363:1107-1116
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute ARDS Clinical Trials Network. Comparison of two fluid-management strategies in acute lung injury (FACTT trial). N Engl J Med 2006; 354:2564-2575
