osces.title: Chronic Cough - Differential Diagnosis and Systematic Investigation
learning_objectives: Apply systematic approach to chronic cough (>8 weeks duration)
Identify common causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, GORD, ACE-inhibitor
Recognize less common causes: bronchiectasis, ILD, lung cancer, pertussis
Formulate investigation plan based on clinical features
Interpret spirometry with bronchodilator challenge for cough-variant asthma
Prescribe empiric trials for upper airway cough syndrome and GORD
Recognize red flags requiring urgent investigation

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Persistent dry cough for 4 months - no response to multiple courses of antibiotics

history.hpi: Ms Williams presents with 4-month history of persistent dry cough. Cough is worse at night (disrupts sleep), and with talking/laughing (interferes with teaching). No sputum production. No haemoptysis. No dyspnoea at rest or on exertion. No chest pain. No wheeze. Denies fever, night sweats, or weight loss. GP has prescribed 3 courses of antibiotics (amoxicillin, doxycycline, azithromycin) with no improvement. CXR 6 weeks ago normal. Patient increasingly frustrated - cough affecting work (students comment on it), causing embarrassment. No recent viral illness preceding cough onset. Reports postnasal drip sensation and frequent throat clearing. Denies heartburn but does report occasional regurgitation of food (especially when bending over).
pmhx: Hypertension (diagnosed 6 months ago, commenced on perindopril 4mg daily)
Allergic rhinitis (seasonal, worse spring/summer, uses cetirizine PRN)

medications.name: Perindopril arginine
medications.frequency: Daily (started 6 months ago - TEMPORAL RELATIONSHIP TO COUGH)

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 2-3 glasses wine per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband and two teenage children in Young
social_history.occupation_details: Primary school teacher (Year 3) for 20 years, exposed to childhood respiratory infections, no occupational irritants

history.family_history: Mother has asthma, father has GORD, no family history of lung cancer or ILD

examination_findings.general: Well-appearing middle-aged female, comfortable at rest, frequent throat clearing during consultation

ent_examination.oropharynx: Mild posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning (suggestive of postnasal drip)

respiratory.auscultation: Vesicular breath sounds bilaterally, no wheeze, no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema

chest_xray.findings: Clear lung fields, normal cardiac size, no masses or infiltrates, no pleural effusion

spirometry_with_bronchodilator_challenge.interpretation: Normal spirometry, no reversible airflow obstruction

peak_expiratory_flow_variability.date: Not performed (could be arranged for 2-week home monitoring if asthma suspected)

full_blood_count.eosinophils: 0.3 × 10⁹/L (normal, not elevated - argues against eosinophilic asthma)

tasks.description: Take focused history to identify potential causes of chronic cough and recognize medication temporal relationship
Formulate differential diagnosis prioritized by clinical features
Interpret spirometry and explain why asthma is unlikely (but not excluded)
Prescribe empiric treatment trial and arrange further investigations as needed
Provide patient education and follow-up plan

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies temporal relationship: Cough started AFTER perindopril commenced 6 months ago (cough onset 4 months ago = 2 months after perindopril)
Asks specifically about ACE-inhibitor cough characteristics (dry, irritating, worse at night, no sputum)
Asks about upper airway symptoms: Postnasal drip (present), throat clearing (present), nasal congestion (allergic rhinitis)
Asks about GORD symptoms: Heartburn (absent), regurgitation (present), cough worse lying down/after meals
Asks about asthma symptoms: Wheeze (absent), dyspnoea (absent), nocturnal waking (cough only, no wheeze), triggers (talking/laughing)

Formulates differential diagnosis: (1) ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (most likely), (2) Upper airway cough syndrome (UACS/postnasal drip), (3) GORD, (4) Cough-variant asthma (less likely - normal spirometry)
Recognizes ACE-inhibitor cough occurs in 10-20% of patients, mechanism: bradykinin accumulation (ACE breaks down bradykinin)
Interprets spirometry: Normal FEV1/FVC ratio (0.82), no reversibility post-bronchodilator (+0.7%, not significant) - argues against classic asthma
States normal spirometry does NOT exclude cough-variant asthma (may have normal baseline spirometry, requires bronchial provocation testing if suspected)
Prescribes intervention #1: STOP perindopril, switch to alternative antihypertensive (angiotensin receptor blocker does NOT cause cough - e.g., irbesartan 150mg daily)
Explains ACE-inhibitor cough may take 1-4 weeks to resolve after cessation (bradykinin levels normalize)
Prescribes intervention #2: Empiric trial for UACS - intranasal corticosteroid (e.g., mometasone furoate 2 sprays each nostril daily, PBS code 8455N) for 4 weeks
Prescribes intervention #3: Empiric trial for GORD - PPI (e.g., esomeprazole 40mg mane, PBS code 8849C) for 8 weeks (GORD-related cough requires higher dose, longer duration)
Justifies empiric trials: Chronic cough often has multiple contributing factors (UACS + GORD common), treating all simultaneously is standard approach
Arranges follow-up in 4 weeks to assess response to ACE-inhibitor cessation + empiric trials

Plans further investigations IF no improvement: (1) 2-week peak flow diary (assess for asthma variability), (2) Methacholine challenge test (bronchial hyper-reactivity), (3) CT chest (exclude bronchiectasis, ILD), (4) Laryngoscopy (vocal cord dysfunction)
Advises lifestyle modifications for GORD: Avoid late meals, elevate head of bed, avoid triggers (coffee, alcohol, chocolate)
Reassures patient: Normal CXR and spirometry exclude serious pathology (lung cancer, ILD), chronic cough is common and usually treatable
Discusses cough suppressants: Generally NOT recommended (don't address underlying cause), codeine linctus only if cough severely affecting sleep and all other measures failed
Safety-netting: Advises patient to return immediately if develops haemoptysis, weight loss, dyspnoea, or chest pain
Communicates clearly and empathetically, acknowledges patient's frustration (4 months of cough, multiple failed antibiotic courses)

osces.clinical_context: Chronic cough (>8 weeks duration) affects 10-20% of adults and is one of the most common reasons for respiratory clinic referral. In non-smokers with normal CXR, the three most common causes are: (1) Upper airway cough syndrome (UACS, formerly postnasal drip syndrome) - 40%, (2) Asthma/cough-variant asthma - 25%, (3) GORD - 20%. ACE-inhibitor cough occurs in 10-20% of patients (more common in females), typically develops 1 week to 6 months after starting medication, and resolves within 1-4 weeks of cessation. ARBs do NOT cause cough. Systematic approach: History → CXR → Spirometry → Empiric trials (treat UACS, GORD, asthma simultaneously) → Specialist investigations if no response (CT chest, methacholine challenge, laryngoscopy, 24hr pH impedance).
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to chronic cough. Strong candidates will identify temporal relationship between perindopril and cough onset (KEY diagnostic clue - cough started 2 months after ACE-inhibitor). Evaluate ability to formulate prioritized differential diagnosis integrating history (postnasal drip, regurgitation) and investigations (normal spirometry). Candidates should recognize ACE-inhibitor cough as most likely and prescribe appropriate switch to ARB. Assess understanding of empiric trial approach for chronic cough (UACS, GORD, asthma treated simultaneously - don't wait for one trial to fail before starting next). Strong candidates will explain when to pursue further investigations (if no response to empiric trials) and recognize role of specialist tests (methacholine challenge, 24hr pH monitoring). Communication skills important - managing patient expectations (may take 4-8 weeks for improvement, cough often multifactorial).

red_flags.flag: Haemoptysis (ANY amount in chronic cough)
red_flags.action: URGENT CT chest, bronchoscopy, exclude lung cancer, bronchiectasis, TB

red_flags.flag: Unintentional weight loss (>5kg) or anorexia with chronic cough
red_flags.action: URGENT CT chest, exclude malignancy, TB, ILD

red_flags.flag: Chronic cough in current/ex-smoker (>10 pack-year history)
red_flags.action: CT chest mandatory (exclude lung cancer), bronchoscopy if abnormal CT

red_flags.flag: Dyspnoea or reduced exercise tolerance with chronic cough
red_flags.action: Spirometry, CT chest, exclude ILD, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension

red_flags.flag: Systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats) with chronic cough
red_flags.action: CXR, sputum AFB smears, QuantiFERON, exclude TB, lymphoma

differential_diagnosis: ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (most likely - temporal relationship, dry cough, perindopril started 6 months ago)
Upper airway cough syndrome / postnasal drip (likely contributing - postnasal drip sensation, throat clearing, allergic rhinitis, posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning)
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (possible - regurgitation present, cough worse lying down)
Cough-variant asthma (less likely - normal spirometry, no wheeze, but cannot exclude without bronchial provocation testing)
Bronchiectasis (unlikely - no sputum production, normal CXR, no history of recurrent infections)
Interstitial lung disease (unlikely - normal CXR, no dyspnoea, no crackles)
Lung cancer (very unlikely - never smoker, normal CXR, no weight loss, no haemoptysis)

osces.title: Occupational Lung Disease - Asbestosis Assessment and Compensation
learning_objectives: Obtain detailed occupational exposure history for asbestos
Recognize clinical and radiological features of asbestosis
Differentiate asbestosis from asbestos-related pleural disease
Interpret HRCT findings in asbestos-related lung disease
Assess respiratory impairment and functional impact
Understand compensation pathways in NSW (icare, Dust Diseases Tribunal)
Recognize increased risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma with asbestos exposure

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Progressive breathlessness over 5 years - HRCT showing interstitial changes, GP suspects asbestosis

history.hpi: Mr Anderson presents with 5-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, now dyspnoeic walking 50 metres on flat ground (mMRC grade 3). Associated with dry cough (no sputum, no haemoptysis). No chest pain. Reports decreased exercise tolerance - previously walked 5km daily, now struggles with 200 metres. No weight loss. No fevers or night sweats. GP ordered HRCT chest 2 weeks ago showing interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques, suspicious for asbestos-related disease. Patient worked as carpenter and builder 1965-2005 (40 years), with extensive asbestos exposure (cutting asbestos-cement sheeting, installing asbestos insulation, demolition work). No respiratory protection used until 1980s. Now seeking assessment for compensation claim.
pmhx: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (metformin 1g BD, gliclazide MR 60mg daily, HbA1c 7.2%)
Previous myocardial infarction 2012 (PCI to LAD, on aspirin + clopidogrel until 2013)

social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, 40 pack-year history (smoked 1 pack/day 1965-2005, quit 20 years ago when retired)
social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 2-3 standard drinks per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife in own home in Young (purchased 1975, house contains asbestos-cement sheeting - patient installed it himself)
social_history.occupation_details: Carpenter and builder 1965-2005 (40 years), EXTENSIVE asbestos exposure: (1) Cutting/drilling asbestos-cement sheeting (fibro sheets) for wall cladding 1965-1980s (daily exposure), (2) Installing asbestos pipe insulation (lagging) in commercial buildings 1970s-1980s, (3) Demolition work 1980s-1990s (disturbing old asbestos materials), (4) No respiratory protection until mid-1980s (disposable masks only from ~1987), (5) Work clothes washed at home by wife (secondary exposure risk). Ceased asbestos work 1990, fully retired 2005.
social_history.support: Wife (also concerned about her secondary exposure)

history.family_history: Father died age 65 (pneumoconiosis - coal miner), mother died age 82 (dementia), no family history of lung cancer or mesothelioma

examination_findings.general: Elderly male, appears well, mild dyspnoea on minimal exertion (walking to examination couch)

vital_signs.spo2: 94% on room air at rest, desaturates to 88% after walking 50 metres

respiratory.auscultation: Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles (Velcro-like), no wheeze

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual with loud P2 (possible pulmonary hypertension), no murmurs, no peripheral oedema

findings.parenchymal: Bilateral basal and subpleural interstitial fibrosis with reticular pattern, subpleural lines, ground-glass opacification in lower lobes, no honeycombing. Pattern consistent with asbestosis (basal-predominant fibrosis in patient with documented asbestos exposure).
findings.pleural: Bilateral calcified pleural plaques (diaphragmatic and lateral chest wall), NO pleural thickening or effusion. Pleural plaques are PATHOGNOMONIC for asbestos exposure.
findings.other: No lung masses, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy

hrct_chest.conclusion: Asbestosis (bilateral basal interstitial fibrosis) + asbestos-related pleural plaques. Findings consistent with significant asbestos exposure.

chest_xray.findings: Bilateral lower zone reticular shadowing, calcified pleural plaques bilateral hemidiaphragms, no masses

pulmonary_function_tests.interpretation: Moderate restrictive ventilatory defect with severe impairment of gas transfer. Pattern consistent with interstitial lung disease (asbestosis).

autoimmune_screen.date: Today (to exclude connective tissue disease-related ILD)

tasks.description: Obtain detailed occupational asbestos exposure history (type, duration, intensity, timing)
Interpret HRCT and PFTs to confirm diagnosis of asbestosis and assess severity
Explain asbestosis diagnosis and differentiate from other asbestos-related diseases
Discuss compensation pathways (icare NSW, Dust Diseases Tribunal) and provide documentation
Counsel on lung cancer/mesothelioma surveillance and management plan

marking_criteria.criterion: Obtains comprehensive asbestos exposure history: Type (asbestos-cement, pipe insulation), duration (1965-1990, 25 years), intensity (daily cutting/drilling, demolition), lack of respiratory protection (until 1987)
Asks about latency period: First asbestos exposure 1965, symptoms started ~2020 = 55-year latency (asbestosis typically 15-40 years post-exposure)
Asks about other asbestos-related diseases: Pleural plaques (present), pleural effusion (absent), mesothelioma symptoms (absent), lung cancer (no masses on CT)
Interprets HRCT: Bilateral basal interstitial fibrosis + pleural plaques = diagnostic of asbestosis in context of asbestos exposure
Recognizes pleural plaques are PATHOGNOMONIC for asbestos exposure (but plaques themselves are benign, do not cause symptoms)
Interprets PFTs: Restrictive pattern (FVC 62% predicted), severely reduced TLCO (42% predicted) - consistent with asbestosis severity
Confirms diagnosis: Asbestosis (documented asbestos exposure + HRCT showing basal fibrosis + restrictive PFTs + exclusion of other ILD causes)
Explains asbestosis to patient: Lung scarring (fibrosis) caused by asbestos fibers inhaled during work, progressive and irreversible
Differentiates asbestosis from pleural plaques: Plaques are benign scarring of pleura (do NOT cause breathlessness), asbestosis is lung parenchymal fibrosis (DOES cause breathlessness)
Discusses smoking as synergistic risk factor: 40 pack-year history + asbestos exposure increases lung cancer risk 50-90x (vs 5x asbestos alone, 10x smoking alone)
Explains compensation eligibility: NSW icare (formerly WorkCover) for occupational lung disease, OR Dust Diseases Tribunal for asbestos-related diseases
States Dust Diseases Tribunal is specialist NSW jurisdiction for asbestos claims (faster processing, medical assessments provided)
Provides medical report/documentation: Detailed occupational history, HRCT report, PFT results, diagnosis (asbestosis), functional impairment assessment (required for compensation claim)
Advises referral to specialist solicitor (asbestos/dust diseases) - most claimants use legal representation for complex compensation process
Discusses lung cancer surveillance: Annual low-dose CT chest screening (high-risk due to asbestos + smoking history), immediate investigation if new symptoms
Discusses mesothelioma risk: Latency 20-50 years post-exposure, annual CXR insufficient (mesothelioma often presents as pleural effusion or pleural mass), CT if new symptoms
Addresses wife's secondary asbestos exposure concern: Washing work clothes at home IS recognized exposure route, should have chest X-ray screening
Discusses management: NO cure for asbestosis, supportive care (pulmonary rehabilitation, ambulatory oxygen, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination)
Arranges pulmonary rehabilitation referral (mMRC grade 3 qualifies)
Arranges ambulatory oxygen assessment (desaturates to 85% on 6MWT, likely requires supplemental oxygen for exertion)
Discusses prognosis: Asbestosis is progressive, rate varies (some stable for years, others progress to respiratory failure), 5-year survival ~80% for mild-moderate disease
Safety-netting: Advises immediate return if: Haemoptysis (lung cancer), chest pain/shortness of breath worsening (pleural effusion/mesothelioma), unintentional weight loss
Communicates empathetically, acknowledges occupational disease context (preventable exposure, employer responsibility)

osces.clinical_context: Asbestos exposure in Australia peaked 1950s-1980s (mining, manufacturing, construction). Over 10,000 Australians die from asbestos-related diseases annually (mesothelioma, lung cancer, asbestosis). Asbestosis is diffuse pulmonary fibrosis caused by asbestos fiber inhalation, latency 15-40 years, dose-dependent (higher exposure = earlier/more severe disease). Diagnosis requires: (1) documented asbestos exposure, (2) HRCT showing basal-predominant interstitial fibrosis, (3) restrictive PFTs, (4) exclusion of other ILD causes. Pleural plaques (benign calcified pleural scarring) are pathognomonic for asbestos exposure but do NOT cause symptoms. Asbestos + smoking synergistically increase lung cancer risk (50-90x vs general population). NSW Dust Diseases Tribunal provides specialist compensation pathway (medical + financial support). No cure; management is supportive (pulmonary rehab, oxygen, vaccinations, cancer surveillance).
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to occupational history (type, duration, intensity, timing of asbestos exposure). Strong candidates will integrate history, HRCT (basal fibrosis + pleural plaques), and PFTs (restrictive, reduced TLCO) to confirm asbestosis diagnosis. Evaluate understanding of differentiation between asbestosis (symptomatic parenchymal fibrosis) and pleural plaques (asymptomatic pleural scarring). Candidates should recognize synergistic smoking risk (40 pack-years + asbestos = 50-90x lung cancer risk) and recommend annual low-dose CT screening. Assess knowledge of NSW-specific compensation pathways (Dust Diseases Tribunal) and ability to provide appropriate medical documentation. Strong candidates will address wife's secondary exposure concern and arrange surveillance. Communication skills critical - discussing progressive incurable disease with occupational context (preventable harm).

red_flags.flag: Pleural effusion (especially bloody) in patient with asbestos exposure
red_flags.action: URGENT investigation for malignant mesothelioma - CT chest, thoracentesis with cytology, respiratory physician/thoracic surgery referral

red_flags.flag: New lung mass or nodule in patient with asbestos exposure + smoking history
red_flags.action: URGENT CT chest with contrast, PET-CT, respiratory physician referral, likely lung cancer (asbestos + smoking synergistic)

red_flags.flag: Progressive respiratory failure in asbestosis (SpO2 <88% at rest, PaCO2 rising)
red_flags.action: Consider long-term oxygen therapy, pulmonary hypertension assessment (echo), discuss advance care planning, palliative care involvement

red_flags.flag: Round atelectasis on HRCT (can mimic lung mass)
red_flags.action: Recognize benign asbestos-related finding (pleural plaque causes adjacent lung collapse), BUT exclude malignancy with PET-CT or biopsy if atypical features

differential_diagnosis: Asbestosis (confirmed diagnosis - documented exposure + HRCT basal fibrosis + restrictive PFTs + pleural plaques)
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (excluded by asbestos exposure history and pleural plaques)
Connective tissue disease-related ILD (excluded by negative autoimmune screen, no extrapulmonary features)
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (excluded by occupational history, no relevant exposures)
key_references: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (eTG complete), Occupational Lung Disease section
Australian Mesothelioma Registry - asbestos exposure assessment and surveillance
NSW Dust Diseases Tribunal - compensation guidelines for asbestosis (www.dustdiseases.nsw.gov.au)
American Thoracic Society. Diagnosis and initial management of nonmalignant diseases related to asbestos. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2004; 170:691-715
icare NSW (formerly WorkCover NSW) - occupational lung disease compensation pathways
National Lung Screening Trial - low-dose CT screening for lung cancer in high-risk groups (asbestos exposure + smoking)

osces.title: Bronchoscopy - Indication Assessment and Informed Consent
learning_objectives: Recognize appropriate indications for bronchoscopy
Assess contraindications and relative contraindications
Explain bronchoscopy procedure to patient using lay terminology
Obtain valid informed consent including risks and complications
Discuss sedation options (conscious sedation vs general anesthesia)
Plan pre-procedure investigations and preparation
Recognize when to perform endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) vs standard bronchoscopy

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW (procedural consent clinic)
scenario.presenting_complaint: Right upper lobe mass on CT chest - referred for bronchoscopy to obtain tissue diagnosis

history.hpi: Ms Schultz presented to GP 6 weeks ago with 3-month history of persistent cough and two episodes of haemoptysis (blood-streaked sputum, total ~10mL). CXR showed right upper lobe opacity. CT chest revealed 3.2cm spiculated mass in right upper lobe with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (right paratracheal nodes up to 2.5cm). PET-CT showed FDG-avid mass (SUVmax 9.5) and mediastinal nodes (SUVmax 7.2), suspicious for lung cancer with N2 nodal involvement. Sputum cytology non-diagnostic. Now referred for bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) for tissue diagnosis and mediastinal staging. Patient anxious about procedure, requesting detailed explanation.
pmhx: Atrial fibrillation (warfarin - target INR 2-3, currently INR 2.4)

allergies.reaction: Nausea and vomiting (intolerance, not true allergy)

social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, 25 pack-year history (smoked 1968-2005, quit 20 years ago)
social_history.alcohol: Nil
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband in Young, adult daughter lives in Sydney
social_history.occupation_details: Librarian for 35 years (retired 10 years ago), no occupational exposures
social_history.support: Husband will accompany to procedure, daughter available if needed

history.family_history: Mother died age 70 (breast cancer), father died age 75 (stroke), no family history of lung cancer

examination_findings.general: Well-appearing elderly female, comfortable at rest, appears anxious about procedure

respiratory.auscultation: Reduced breath sounds right upper zone, no wheeze, no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Irregularly irregular pulse (AF), HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema

airway_assessment.dentition: Full upper and lower dentition, some loose lower teeth (potential aspiration risk during bronchoscopy)
airway_assessment.conclusion: Low risk for difficult intubation if general anesthesia required, but loose teeth require careful bronchoscope insertion

findings.primary_mass: 3.2cm spiculated mass right upper lobe (anterior segment), abutting chest wall, no rib destruction
findings.lymph_nodes: Enlarged right paratracheal lymph nodes (station 4R, largest 2.5cm), right hilar nodes (station 10R, 1.8cm), subcarinal node (station 7, 1.2cm)
findings.metastases: No liver lesions, no adrenal masses, no bone lesions

findings.primary_mass: Right upper lobe mass SUVmax 9.5 (highly FDG-avid, consistent with malignancy)
findings.lymph_nodes: Right paratracheal (4R) SUVmax 7.2, right hilar (10R) SUVmax 6.5, subcarinal (7) SUVmax 5.8 - all pathological, suggests N2 disease

coagulation.inr: 2.4 (therapeutic for AF, but ELEVATED for procedural risk)

ecg.findings: Atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 70-85 bpm, no ST/T changes

pulmonary_function_tests.interpretation: Mild restrictive pattern, adequate respiratory reserve for bronchoscopy

tasks.description: Explain indication for bronchoscopy with EBUS (tissue diagnosis and mediastinal staging)
Explain bronchoscopy procedure step-by-step using lay terminology
Discuss risks and complications to obtain valid informed consent
Address warfarin management and plan pre-procedure preparation
Answer patient questions and provide post-procedure instructions

marking_criteria.criterion: Explains indication: Lung mass on CT requires tissue diagnosis (biopsy) to confirm if cancer and determine type (guides treatment)
Explains EBUS component: Enlarged lymph nodes in chest (mediastinum) need sampling to determine if cancer has spread (staging)
States EBUS-TBNA is minimally invasive alternative to mediastinoscopy (surgical procedure) for mediastinal staging
Explains bronchoscopy procedure: Flexible tube (diameter ~6mm) with camera passed through nose or mouth into airways (bronchi) while patient sedated
Describes sedation: Conscious sedation (midazolam + fentanyl IV) - patient sleepy but breathing independently, OR general anesthesia if patient prefers (fully asleep)
Explains local anesthesia: Throat and airways sprayed with local anesthetic (lignocaine) to suppress cough reflex and improve comfort
Describes biopsy technique: Small samples (biopsies) taken from lung mass using forceps passed through bronchoscope
Describes EBUS-TBNA: Ultrasound probe on bronchoscope tip visualizes lymph nodes, needle passed through airway wall to sample nodes (transbronchial needle aspiration)
Explains duration: Procedure takes 30-45 minutes, plus 1-2 hours recovery (total 2-3 hours in hospital)
Discusses common side effects: Sore throat (2-3 days), hoarse voice (temporary), cough (few days), blood-tinged sputum (small amount normal for 24 hours)
Discusses serious complications: Bleeding (1-2% risk, higher with biopsies), pneumothorax (1-2% risk if transbronchial biopsies), respiratory depression from sedation (<1%), infection (<1%)
Quantifies bleeding risk: Minor bleeding common (blood-tinged sputum), significant bleeding rare (<1%), massive bleeding very rare (<0.1%)
Addresses warfarin: INR 2.4 is ELEVATED for bronchoscopy with biopsies (target INR <1.5 for endobronchial biopsies, <1.2 for TBNA per BTS guidelines)

Plans warfarin management: STOP warfarin 5 days pre-procedure, check INR day before (target <1.5), bridge with LMWH if CHA₂DS₂-VASc high (patient has AF + age 65 = score 2, moderate risk - bridging recommended)
Explains bridging: LMWH (enoxaparin) injections subcutaneous while warfarin held, last dose 24 hours pre-procedure, restart warfarin evening of procedure
Advises NBM (nil by mouth): Nothing to eat 6 hours pre-procedure, sips water until 2 hours before (aspiration risk during sedation)
Arranges escort: Patient MUST have responsible adult to take home (cannot drive or operate machinery for 24 hours post-sedation)
Post-procedure instructions: No eating/drinking for 2 hours (until throat sensation returns), avoid hot liquids for 24 hours, no driving for 24 hours
Safety-netting post-procedure: Return immediately if: Significant haemoptysis (>2 tablespoons blood), chest pain, severe dyspnoea, fever >38°C
Discusses biopsy results timeline: Preliminary pathology 2-3 days, full report (including molecular testing if cancer) 7-10 days, follow-up appointment scheduled
Addresses loose teeth concern: Explains bronchoscope will be inserted carefully to avoid dislodging teeth, but dental trauma possible (rare, <0.1%)
Obtains informed consent: Checks patient understanding ('Can you tell me in your own words what the procedure involves?'), answers questions, confirms patient willing to proceed
Communicates empathetically, acknowledges anxiety, reassures about safety (common procedure, performed regularly, experienced team)
Documents consent: Completes written consent form, includes discussion of risks, confirms patient capacity to consent

osces.clinical_context: Bronchoscopy is the most common procedure in respiratory medicine, performed for diagnostic (tissue sampling, BAL) and therapeutic (foreign body removal, stent insertion) indications. Flexible bronchoscopy via transnasal or transoral route under conscious sedation (midazolam + fentanyl) is standard. EBUS-TBNA (endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration) allows real-time ultrasound-guided sampling of mediastinal lymph nodes via bronchoscope, replacing surgical mediastinoscopy in most cases (sensitivity ~90% for N2 staging). Complications: bleeding 1-2%, pneumothorax 1-2% (higher with transbronchial biopsies), respiratory depression <1%. Anticoagulation requires careful management: stop warfarin 5 days pre-procedure (target INR <1.5 for endobronchial biopsies), bridging LMWH if high thrombotic risk. Australian guidelines (TSANZ/BTS) recommend INR <1.2 for TBNA due to higher bleeding risk.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's ability to explain complex procedure using lay terminology and obtain valid informed consent. Strong candidates will describe bronchoscopy step-by-step (sedation, local anesthetic, bronchoscope insertion, biopsy, EBUS-TBNA) in patient-friendly language. Evaluate understanding of complication risks (bleeding 1-2%, pneumothorax 1-2%) and ability to quantify these to patient. Critical assessment point: warfarin management - candidates MUST recognize INR 2.4 is too high for bronchoscopy with biopsies and plan appropriate warfarin cessation + LMWH bridging (AF patient with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 requires bridging). Strong candidates will provide comprehensive pre-procedure instructions (NBM, escort required, medication adjustments) and post-procedure safety-netting. Communication skills paramount - obtaining informed consent requires checking patient understanding, answering questions, and respecting autonomy.

red_flags.flag: Massive haemoptysis post-bronchoscopy (>50mL bright red blood)
red_flags.action: Position patient bleeding side down, 100% oxygen, urgent CT chest, interventional radiology for bronchial artery embolization, thoracic surgery consult

red_flags.flag: Pneumothorax post-bronchoscopy (sudden chest pain, dyspnoea, absent breath sounds)
red_flags.action: Urgent CXR, if tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS MCL), chest tube insertion

red_flags.flag: Respiratory depression during sedation (SpO2 <85%, apnoeic)
red_flags.action: Airway support (jaw thrust, bag-mask ventilation), reverse sedation (flumazenil for midazolam, naloxone for fentanyl), consider endotracheal intubation

red_flags.flag: Laryngospasm during bronchoscopy (stridor, unable to ventilate)
red_flags.action: Remove bronchoscope, 100% oxygen, positive pressure ventilation, if refractory → small dose propofol or suxamethonium + intubation

differential_diagnosis: Not applicable (bronchoscopy is diagnostic procedure, not diagnosis)

Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) Guidelines for Bronchoscopy
Du Rand IA et al. British Thoracic Society guideline for advanced diagnostic and therapeutic flexible bronchoscopy in adults. Thorax 2011; 66(Suppl 3):iii1-iii21

Douketis JD et al. Perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy: Antithrombotic Therapy and Prevention of Thrombosis, 9th ed: American College of Chest Physicians Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines. Chest 2012; 141(2 Suppl):e326S-e350S
Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists (ANZCA) Guidelines for Procedural Sedation
Yarmus L, Feller-Kopman D. Bronchoscopy for lung cancer staging. Curr Opin Pulm Med 2014; 20(4):321-326

osces.title: Pulmonary Hypertension - Right Heart Catheterization Interpretation
objectives: Interpret right heart catheterization haemodynamic measurements
Classify pulmonary hypertension according to WHO functional class
Initiate appropriate targeted therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Assess right ventricular function and cardiac output
Explain vasoreactivity testing and treatment implications
Discuss prognosis and referral for advanced therapies
osces.scenario_stem: You are a medical registrar in the respiratory clinic at a tertiary hospital. Ms Jennifer Walsh, a 52-year-old woman, presents with progressive dyspnoea (NYHA Class III) and has recently undergone right heart catheterization for suspected pulmonary hypertension. Her echocardiogram showed severe pulmonary hypertension (estimated RVSP 85 mmHg) with right ventricular dilatation and impaired function (TAPSE 14 mm). She has no history of left heart disease, chronic lung disease, or thromboembolic disease. The right heart catheterization was performed yesterday. Review the catheterization results, classify her pulmonary hypertension, discuss treatment options, and explain prognosis.

patient_demographics.living_situation: Lives with husband in suburban Sydney

presenting_complaint.chief_complaint: Progressive shortness of breath over 18 months, reduced exercise tolerance, occasional chest tightness
presenting_complaint.severity: Unable to climb stairs without stopping, previously very active (played tennis regularly)
presenting_complaint.pattern: Progressive, worse with exertion, some improvement with rest
associated_symptoms: No chest pain, cough, or haemoptysis
presenting_complaint.impact_on_life: Stopped working 3 months ago due to fatigue and breathlessness, unable to play tennis, struggles with household activities

history_of_presenting_complaint.onset: Gradual onset 18 months ago, initially attributed to deconditioning and stress
history_of_presenting_complaint.progression: Progressive worsening despite initial attempts at exercise rehabilitation
history_of_presenting_complaint.precipitating_factors: No clear precipitant, symptoms worse with any physical exertion
history_of_presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: Rest provides partial relief, no response to bronchodilators (tried by GP)
history_of_presenting_complaint.investigations_to_date: Echocardiogram showed RVSP 85 mmHg, right ventricular dilatation, TAPSE 14 mm, normal left ventricular function (EF 60%), no significant valvular disease. CT pulmonary angiogram excluded chronic thromboembolic disease. High-resolution CT chest showed no interstitial lung disease. Spirometry normal (FEV1/FVC 0.82, FEV1 95% predicted). NT-proBNP elevated at 1,850 pg/mL. 6-minute walk distance 280 metres with oxygen desaturation to 89%.
history_of_presenting_complaint.treatments_tried: Salbutamol inhaler (no benefit), low-dose frusemide 20 mg daily (minimal benefit), ceased due to postural hypotension

conditions: Raynaud's phenomenon (15 years, managed conservatively)
Positive anti-centromere antibodies (tested 5 years ago for Raynaud's)
Mild oesophageal dysmotility on barium swallow (limited systemic sclerosis suspected)
No history of appetite suppressant use
No HIV risk factors
No liver disease
hospitalisations: Admission 6 weeks ago for right heart catheterization workup

conditions: Mother: Systemic sclerosis (died age 68 from pulmonary complications)
Father: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes (alive, age 78)
Sister: Raynaud's phenomenon
No family history of congenital heart disease or sudden cardiac death
family_history.genetic_risk: Significant family history of connective tissue disease

occupation.current: On sick leave from primary school teaching
occupation.exposure: No occupational exposures to lung toxins

exercise.baseline: Previously very active - tennis 3x/week, walking daily

social_history.living_environment: Suburban house, no mould or environmental exposures

physical_examination.general_inspection: Well-groomed woman, appears mildly dyspnoeic at rest, comfortable sitting. No cyanosis. No digital clubbing. Positive Raynaud's phenomenon (pale, then cyanotic fingers with cold exposure). Telangiectasia on face and hands.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 94% on room air at rest (drops to 89% with minimal exertion)

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP elevated to 6 cm above sternal angle at 45 degrees. Prominent V waves visible. Slight peripheral oedema (1+ pitting to mid-calf bilaterally).
cardiovascular.palpation: Apex beat not displaced. Palpable right ventricular heave at left sternal edge. Normal volume radial pulses bilaterally, regular rhythm.
cardiovascular.auscultation: Heart sounds: Normal S1, loud P2 (pulmonary component of second heart sound). Pansystolic murmur grade 2/6 at left lower sternal edge (tricuspid regurgitation), louder on inspiration. No diastolic murmurs.

respiratory.inspection: Normal chest wall movement, no use of accessory muscles. Trachea central. No scars.
respiratory.palpation: Normal expansion bilaterally. No tenderness. Tactile fremitus normal.
respiratory.auscultation: Vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. No wheeze, crackles, or pleural rub. Good air entry to bases.

abdominal.inspection: Soft, no distension. Cholecystectomy scars visible.
abdominal.palpation: Liver edge palpable 2 cm below right costal margin, smooth, non-tender, pulsatile (tricuspid regurgitation). No splenomegaly. No ascites.

physical_examination.neurological: Alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Normal power, tone, reflexes, and sensation in all limbs. Gait not assessed due to dyspnoea.
physical_examination.skin: Telangiectasia on face and hands. Mild sclerodactyly (thickened skin on fingers). No rashes or ulcers.
physical_examination.other: Sclerodactyly present. Limited mouth opening (microstomia) - 4 cm interincisor distance (normal >5 cm). Dry mucous membranes.

imaging.result: Right ventricle severely dilated with impaired systolic function (TAPSE 14 mm, normal >17 mm). Right atrium moderately dilated. Estimated right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) 85 mmHg based on tricuspid regurgitation jet. Moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Left ventricle normal size and function (LVEF 60%). No left atrial dilatation. No significant valvular disease. No pericardial effusion. IVC dilated (2.4 cm) with <50% inspiratory collapse (elevated right atrial pressure).
imaging.interpretation: Severe pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure

imaging.result: No evidence of acute or chronic pulmonary embolism. No filling defects. Main pulmonary artery diameter 32 mm (dilated, normal <29 mm). Right ventricle dilated relative to left ventricle (RV/LV ratio 1.4). Patent pulmonary arteries. No interstitial lung disease. No emphysema. Small bilateral pleural effusions.
imaging.interpretation: Excludes chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Confirms pulmonary hypertension.

imaging.result: No evidence of interstitial lung disease. No honeycombing, ground-glass opacification, or reticular abnormality. Minimal basal atelectasis. Dilated pulmonary artery. Enlarged right heart chambers. No bronchiectasis. No emphysema.
imaging.interpretation: Excludes parenchymal lung disease as cause of pulmonary hypertension

imaging.result: Enlarged main pulmonary artery segment. Enlarged right heart border. Clear lung fields. No consolidation or pulmonary oedema. Cardiothoracic ratio 0.54 (mildly increased).
imaging.interpretation: Consistent with pulmonary hypertension and right heart enlargement

laboratory.interpretation: Markedly elevated - indicates right ventricular strain and heart failure

laboratory.result: Bilirubin 22 μmol/L (3-20), ALT 28 U/L (5-40), AST 32 U/L (5-40), ALP 88 U/L (30-110), Albumin 38 g/L (35-50). GGT 35 U/L (5-55).
laboratory.interpretation: Mild hyperbilirubinaemia (congestive hepatopathy from right heart failure). Otherwise normal.

laboratory.result: Creatinine 72 μmol/L (45-90), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m². Urea 5.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5).
ANA positive 1:640 (centromere pattern). Anti-centromere antibodies strongly positive. Rheumatoid factor negative. Anti-Scl-70 negative. Anti-RNA polymerase III negative.
laboratory.interpretation: Strongly positive anti-centromere antibodies - diagnostic of limited systemic sclerosis (lcSSc). Pattern associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension.

pulmonary_function.result: FEV1 2.85 L (95% predicted), FVC 3.48 L (97% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.82 (normal >0.70). No significant bronchodilator response.
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Normal spirometry - excludes obstructive or restrictive lung disease

pulmonary_function.result: Total lung capacity (TLC) 4.8 L (92% predicted), Residual volume (RV) 1.3 L (88% predicted). RV/TLC ratio 0.27 (normal <0.35).
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Normal lung volumes - excludes interstitial lung disease
Reduced diffusion capacity - consistent with pulmonary vascular disease

pulmonary_function.result: Distance 280 metres (predicted >500 metres for age/gender). Baseline SpO2 94%, nadir SpO2 89% (>4% desaturation). Borg dyspnoea score at end: 7/10. Heart rate increase from 88 to 128 bpm.

haemodynamics.result: Right atrial pressure (RAP) 12 mmHg (normal 0-5 mmHg). Right ventricular pressure 78/12 mmHg. Pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) 78/32 mmHg, mean PAP 52 mmHg (normal <20 mmHg). Pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) 10 mmHg (normal 6-12 mmHg). Cardiac output (Fick method) 3.8 L/min. Cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m² (normal 2.5-4.0 L/min/m²). Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) 11.1 Wood units (normal <2 Wood units). Systemic vascular resistance 18 Wood units. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) 58% (normal 65-75%). Vasoreactivity testing with inhaled nitric oxide (20 ppm for 5 minutes): PAP decreased to 68/28 mmHg, mean PAP 46 mmHg (12% reduction, but did not meet positive vasoreactivity criteria of ≥10 mmHg decrease and mean PAP <40 mmHg). Cardiac output increased to 4.2 L/min.
haemodynamics.interpretation: SEVERE PRE-CAPILLARY PULMONARY HYPERTENSION: Mean PAP 52 mmHg (diagnostic threshold >20 mmHg), normal PAWP 10 mmHg (excludes post-capillary/left heart disease), PVR markedly elevated at 11.1 WU (diagnostic threshold >2 WU). Classification: WHO Group 1 Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) associated with connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis). WHO Functional Class III. Negative vasoreactivity test (not candidate for calcium channel blocker monotherapy). Reduced cardiac output and cardiac index indicate right ventricular failure. Elevated RAP and reduced SvO2 indicate poor prognosis markers.

Limited systemic sclerosis: anti-centromere antibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia

Excluded other causes: normal spirometry/lung volumes, no CTEPH on CTPA, no left heart disease

against_features: CTPA showed no filling defects or chronic thromboembolic changes
No history of previous venous thromboembolism

Echocardiogram: normal left ventricular size and function (EF 60%)
No left atrial dilatation, no significant valvular disease

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Pulmonary Hypertension due to lung disease/hypoxia - WHO Group 3
against_features: Normal spirometry (FEV1/FVC 0.82, no obstruction or restriction)

PVR 11.1 WU far exceeds typical Group 3 (usually mild elevation <5 WU)
Oxygen saturation only mildly reduced at rest (94%)

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Idiopathic Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (IPAH) - WHO Group 1
against_features: Presence of connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis) makes this secondary PAH
Positive anti-centromere antibodies establish CTD-PAH diagnosis
Classification: PAH associated with connective tissue disease, not idiopathic

clinical_reasoning_points: RIGHT HEART CATHETERIZATION is the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension and is MANDATORY for confirming the diagnosis and guiding treatment decisions
Diagnostic criteria for pulmonary hypertension: mean PAP >20 mmHg (updated from previous threshold of ≥25 mmHg in 2018 guidelines)
PRE-CAPILLARY vs POST-CAPILLARY distinction is critical: PAWP ≤15 mmHg indicates pre-capillary (Groups 1, 3, 4, 5), PAWP >15 mmHg indicates post-capillary (Group 2 - left heart disease)
PVR >2 Wood units confirms pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (in addition to elevated PAP and normal PAWP)

WHO Classification: Group 1 (PAH - includes idiopathic, hereditary, drug-induced, connective tissue disease-associated, congenital heart disease, portal hypertension), Group 2 (left heart disease), Group 3 (lung disease/hypoxia), Group 4 (CTEPH), Group 5 (unclear/multifactorial)

LIMITED SYSTEMIC SCLEROSIS (lcSSc) has HIGHEST prevalence of PAH among connective tissue diseases (10-15% develop PAH). Anti-centromere antibodies are hallmark of lcSSc and associated with higher PAH risk.

VASOREACTIVITY TESTING with inhaled nitric oxide, IV epoprostenol, or IV adenosine identifies patients who may respond to calcium channel blockers (CCBs). Positive test: ≥10 mmHg decrease in mean PAP to absolute value <40 mmHg, with increased or unchanged cardiac output. Only 10-15% of IPAH patients are vasoreactive, even fewer in CTD-PAH.
This patient's vasoreactivity test was NEGATIVE (mean PAP decreased by 6 mmHg to 46 mmHg, did not reach <40 mmHg threshold), so CCB monotherapy is contraindicated. She requires PAH-targeted therapy.

PROGNOSTIC FACTORS in PAH: Poor prognosis indicated by WHO FC III-IV, 6MWD <300m, elevated RAP >8 mmHg, low cardiac index <2.5 L/min/m², elevated NT-proBNP, low SvO2 <65%. This patient has MULTIPLE poor prognostic markers.

Australian PBS criteria for PAH therapies (endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues, soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators) require: 1) Diagnosis confirmed by RHC, 2) WHO Group 1 PAH, 3) WHO FC II-IV, 4) Prescribed by or in consultation with specialist with expertise in PAH

INITIAL COMBINATION THERAPY (two drugs upfront) is now recommended for intermediate-high and high-risk PAH patients (2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines). Regimen: endothelin receptor antagonist + phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (e.g., ambrisentan + tadalafil, or macitentan + tadalafil).
CTD-PAH patients have WORSE prognosis than IPAH, with 3-year survival 50-60% vs 65-70% for IPAH. Aggressive treatment and early referral to advanced therapy centres are critical.

MONITORING: Serial 6MWT, NT-proBNP, echocardiography every 3-6 months. Repeat RHC at 3-6 months to assess treatment response. Goal: achieve low-risk status (WHO FC I-II, 6MWD >440m, NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL, RAP <8 mmHg, cardiac index ≥2.5 L/min/m²).

ADVANCED THERAPIES for refractory PAH: IV/subcutaneous prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol, treprostinil), lung transplantation. Refer to specialist PAH centre if inadequate response to oral dual therapy within 3-6 months.

SUPPORTIVE MEASURES: Diuretics for fluid overload (frusemide, cautiously to avoid reducing cardiac preload excessively), oxygen therapy if SpO2 <90%, warfarin anticoagulation is CONTROVERSIAL in CTD-PAH (benefit less clear than IPAH, bleeding risk with oesophageal varices if portal hypertension develops). Exercise training in supervised pulmonary rehabilitation improves functional capacity.
CTD-PAH screening: All systemic sclerosis patients should have ANNUAL echocardiography screening for PAH, starting at diagnosis. Earlier detection improves outcomes.

red_flags.flag: Severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with right heart failure (WHO FC III, elevated RAP, low cardiac index, reduced SvO2)
red_flags.action: Urgent initiation of PAH-specific therapy. Refer to specialist PAH centre. Risk of right heart decompensation and sudden cardiac death.

red_flags.flag: Multiple poor prognostic markers (RAP 12 mmHg, cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m², SvO2 58%, 6MWD 280m, NT-proBNP 1850 pg/mL)
red_flags.action: High-risk patient. Requires aggressive upfront combination therapy (dual oral therapy) and close monitoring. Consider early evaluation for advanced therapies (parenteral prostanoids, lung transplantation).

red_flags.flag: Connective tissue disease-associated PAH (limited systemic sclerosis) - worse prognosis than idiopathic PAH
red_flags.action: CTD-PAH has higher mortality than IPAH. Requires multidisciplinary care (rheumatology, respiratory, cardiology). Monitor for other organ involvement (renal crisis, ILD progression).

red_flags.flag: Negative vasoreactivity test - calcium channel blocker monotherapy contraindicated
red_flags.action: Do NOT use CCBs alone (risk of hypotension and worsening right heart failure in non-vasoreactive patients). Requires PAH-targeted therapy.

osces.title: Cystic Fibrosis - Multidisciplinary Management and CFTR Modulators
objectives: Assess acute exacerbation of cystic fibrosis and prescribe appropriate antibiotics
Optimize airway clearance, nutritional support, and pancreatic enzyme replacement
Discuss eligibility for CFTR modulator therapy and expected benefits
Coordinate multidisciplinary care (respiratory, dietetics, physiotherapy, psychology)
Address complications: diabetes, liver disease, reduced fertility
Discuss lung transplantation referral criteria and timing

clinical_context.setting: Adult cystic fibrosis clinic, tertiary hospital

osces.scenario_stem: You are a respiratory medicine registrar in the adult cystic fibrosis (CF) clinic at a tertiary hospital. Mr Daniel Kim, a 28-year-old man with cystic fibrosis (homozygous F508del mutation), presents with an acute pulmonary exacerbation. He reports increased cough, sputum production (green, purulent), fatigue, and weight loss (3 kg over 2 weeks). His FEV1 today is 38% predicted (baseline 48% predicted). He has chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization and CF-related diabetes. He is interested in CFTR modulator therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor), which has recently become PBS-listed for F508del homozygous patients. Assess the exacerbation, initiate treatment, discuss CFTR modulator eligibility, and coordinate multidisciplinary care.

pulmonary_function.interpretation: Chronic hypoxic respiratory failure. Meets criteria for long-term oxygen therapy. Worsened during exacerbation (increased O2 requirement).

microbiology.result: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization (every sample positive). Mucoid phenotype. Previous antibiotic sensitivities: Resistant to ciprofloxacin, amoxicillin/clavulanate. Sensitive to piperacillin/tazobactam, tobramycin, meropenem, ceftazidime, colistin. No methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) isolated in past 2 years. Aspergillus fumigatus isolated once (18 months ago, treated for ABPA, resolved).
microbiology.interpretation: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization with developing antibiotic resistance (fluoroquinolone-resistant). Requires IV combination antibiotics for exacerbations (two anti-pseudomonal agents for synergy).

other.result: Homozygous F508del mutation (c.1521_1523delCTT; p.Phe508del on both CFTR alleles)
other.interpretation: Most common CF mutation worldwide (~70% of CF alleles). Homozygous F508del patients are ELIGIBLE for elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) CFTR modulator therapy (PBS-listed in Australia since 2020 for age ≥6 years with at least one F508del mutation).

other.result: Lumbar spine T-score -1.8 (osteopenia). Femoral neck T-score -1.4 (osteopenia).
other.interpretation: Osteopenia (T-score between -1.0 and -2.5). Risk factors: malabsorption, vitamin D deficiency, chronic corticosteroid use (not current), hypogonadism, chronic disease. Requires calcium, vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise.

key_findings: Acute pulmonary exacerbation of cystic fibrosis: increased cough, purulent sputum, FEV1 decline (48% to 38%), fever, CRP 68 mg/L, new CXR infiltrate (RUL)
Homozygous F508del mutation - ELIGIBLE for CFTR modulator therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor)
Advanced CF lung disease: FEV1 baseline 48% predicted, extensive bronchiectasis, chronic hypoxic respiratory failure (LTOT)
CF-related liver disease (elevated transaminases, GGT, hepatomegaly, hypoalbuminaemia)
Nutritional compromise: BMI 19.7 kg/m², weight loss 3 kg in 2 weeks, hypoalbuminaemia
Osteopenia (T-score -1.8, vitamin D insufficiency despite supplementation)
Psychosocial challenges: depression/anxiety, reduced work capacity, concerns about future/relationships

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Acute Pulmonary Exacerbation of Cystic Fibrosis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
supporting_features: Increased respiratory symptoms (cough, purulent sputum, dyspnoea)
Systemic symptoms (fever 37.9°C, weight loss 3 kg, fatigue)
Lung function decline (FEV1 48% to 38%, 10% absolute drop)
Inflammatory markers elevated (WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.8, CRP 68 mg/L)
New radiographic changes (RUL consolidation on CXR)
Sputum culture: heavy growth Pseudomonas aeruginosa (chronic colonization, now exacerbation)
Meets Fuchs criteria for CF pulmonary exacerbation (≥4 of 12 criteria present)

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA) - complication of CF
differential_diagnosis.likelihood: LESS LIKELY (previously treated, currently no evidence)
supporting_features: History of Aspergillus fumigatus isolation (18 months ago, treated)
CF patients at increased risk of ABPA (prevalence 10-15%)
against_features: No eosinophilia on FBC (eosinophils not elevated)
No new pulmonary infiltrates suggestive of ABPA (no fleeting opacities, mucus plugging)
Total IgE not elevated (last checked 18 months ago, normal after ABPA treatment)
Aspergillus-specific IgE negative (18 months ago)
Not currently meeting ABPA diagnostic criteria (requires elevated IgE, eosinophilia, Aspergillus serology)

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Pneumothorax (complication of CF, bullous lung disease)
supporting_features: CF patients with advanced disease and bullae at risk of pneumothorax
against_features: No sudden onset pleuritic chest pain
CXR shows no pneumothorax
No unilateral hyperresonance or reduced breath sounds (signs bilateral)

supporting_features: History of massive haemoptysis age 19 (required bronchial artery embolization)
against_features: No haemoptysis reported currently
Sputum is purulent (green), not blood-stained
No significant drop in haemoglobin

clinical_reasoning_points: CYSTIC FIBROSIS is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene (chromosome 7), encoding the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein (chloride channel). Defective CFTR leads to thick, viscous secretions in lungs, pancreas, liver, intestines, and reproductive tract.

F508DEL MUTATION is the most common CF mutation (present in ~70% of CF alleles worldwide). It causes misfolding and degradation of CFTR protein, preventing it from reaching the cell membrane. Homozygous F508del patients have SEVERE disease phenotype.

ACUTE PULMONARY EXACERBATION is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in CF. Defined by Fuchs criteria (≥4 of 12 symptoms/signs): increased cough, sputum production/change, dyspnoea, malaise/fatigue, fever, anorexia/weight loss, sinus pain/tenderness, change in sinus discharge, physical exam findings (crackles/wheeze), FEV1 decline ≥10%, CXR changes, leukocytosis.

PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA is the dominant pathogen in adult CF (chronic colonization in 60-80% of adults). Develops mucoid phenotype (biofilm production), difficult to eradicate. Chronic infection associated with accelerated lung function decline, increased exacerbations, higher mortality.

IV ANTIBIOTIC TREATMENT for CF exacerbations requires TWO anti-pseudomonal agents (synergistic effect, prevent resistance). Common combinations: piperacillin/tazobactam + tobramycin, ceftazidime + tobramycin, meropenem + tobramycin. Duration: 14 days (minimum, may extend to 21 days if slow response). Dose based on previous sensitivities.

CFTR MODULATOR THERAPY represents a paradigm shift in CF treatment - addresses the UNDERLYING DEFECT (corrects CFTR protein function) rather than treating symptoms. Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta): Triple combination highly effective for F508del homozygous and heterozygous patients.

PBS CRITERIA for elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) in Australia: Age ≥6 years, confirmed CF diagnosis, CFTR genotype with at least one F508del mutation (homozygous or heterozygous), FEV1 <90% predicted OR pancreatic insufficiency. Authority prescription required, must be prescribed by CF specialist. Cost: ~$250,000/year (PBS-subsidized, patient pays standard PBS co-payment).

EXPECTED BENEFITS of CFTR modulators in F508del homozygous patients: Absolute FEV1 improvement 10-14 percentage points, reduced pulmonary exacerbations (50-60% reduction), weight gain (2-4 kg), improved quality of life, sweat chloride normalization, potential to delay/prevent need for lung transplantation. Onset: within 4-12 weeks.

MULTIDISCIPLINARY CF CARE is essential: Respiratory physician (coordination), CF nurse specialist (education, adherence), physiotherapist (airway clearance techniques), dietitian (high-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme optimization), psychologist (mental health support), endocrinologist (CFRD management), social worker (disability support, employment).

AIRWAY CLEARANCE is a cornerstone of CF management. Techniques: Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) devices, high-frequency chest wall oscillation (The Vest), autogenic drainage, Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT). Recommended: ≥2 sessions/day when well, increased frequency during exacerbations (3-4 sessions/day).

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT: CF patients require 120-150% of normal caloric intake (increased energy expenditure from increased work of breathing, chronic infection). Target BMI >22 kg/m² for adults (associated with better lung function, survival). Pancreatic enzyme replacement essential (90% of CF patients have pancreatic insufficiency). Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) supplementation required.

CF-RELATED DIABETES (CFRD) prevalence: 20% by age 20, 50% by age 30. Pathophysiology: Pancreatic fibrosis and fatty infiltration → insulin deficiency (NOT insulin resistance like Type 2 DM). Management: Insulin therapy (basal-bolus regimen), carbohydrate counting. HbA1c target <7% (<53 mmol/mol). Annual OGTT screening from age 10.

CF-RELATED LIVER DISEASE: Spectrum from hepatic steatosis to biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Prevalence: 20-30% of CF adults. Monitoring: Annual LFTs, ultrasound every 1-2 years, endoscopy for varices if cirrhosis/portal hypertension. Treatment: Ursodeoxycholic acid (improves bile flow), manage portal hypertension complications.

LUNG TRANSPLANTATION REFERRAL CRITERIA: FEV1 <30% predicted, rapid lung function decline despite optimal therapy, increasing frequency/severity of exacerbations requiring ICU, refractory pneumothorax, massive haemoptysis. Timing: Refer when FEV1 approaching 30% (median wait time 6-12 months in Australia). Post-transplant 5-year survival ~60%.

CONTRACEPTION AND FERTILITY COUNSELLING: Males with CF are 98% infertile due to congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD). Sperm production normal, can father children via assisted reproductive technology (testicular sperm extraction + IVF/ICSI). Females have reduced fertility (thick cervical mucus), but many conceive naturally. Pregnancy in CF requires multidisciplinary care (high-risk obstetrics, CF team), best outcomes if FEV1 >50% and good nutrition pre-conception.

red_flags.flag: FEV1 baseline 48% predicted (severe lung disease, approaching transplant referral threshold of <30%)
red_flags.action: Discuss lung transplantation candidacy and timing with patient. Refer to transplant centre for evaluation if FEV1 continues to decline despite CFTR modulators and optimal management.

red_flags.flag: Chronic hypoxic respiratory failure (baseline SpO2 93-94% on 2 L/min O2, nocturnal desaturations)
red_flags.action: Continue long-term oxygen therapy. Ensure adequate oxygen prescription (2 L/min continuous, increased to 4 L/min during exacerbation). Monitor for CO2 retention (consider ABG if drowsy, confusion develops).

red_flags.flag: Significant weight loss (3 kg in 2 weeks, BMI 19.7 kg/m²) and hypoalbuminaemia (32 g/L)
red_flags.action: Urgent dietitian review. Optimize nutrition: high-calorie oral supplements, consider nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding if unable to maintain weight with oral intake. Optimize pancreatic enzyme replacement (increase dose if steatorrhea). IV nutrition during exacerbation if inadequate oral intake.

red_flags.flag: Suboptimal diabetes control (HbA1c 7.8%, target <7%) during exacerbation
red_flags.action: Acute illness and infection worsen hyperglycaemia. Increase insulin doses during exacerbation. Frequent blood glucose monitoring (4-6 times/day). Endocrinology/diabetes educator input. Optimize control before starting CFTR modulators (can affect glucose metabolism).

red_flags.flag: Fluoroquinolone-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (previous cultures resistant to ciprofloxacin)
red_flags.action: Use IV combination therapy (piperacillin/tazobactam + tobramycin) based on previous sensitivities. Avoid oral fluoroquinolones (ineffective). Monitor tobramycin levels (nephrotoxic, ototoxic). Tailor antibiotics when final sensitivities available.

red_flags.flag: CF-related liver disease with hepatomegaly and hypoalbuminaemia (potential portal hypertension)
red_flags.action: Continue ursodeoxycholic acid. Monitor for varices (last endoscopy 12 months ago, repeat if clinical deterioration). Avoid hepatotoxic drugs. Monitor INR, albumin (synthetic function). Refer hepatology if liver function worsens.

red_flags.flag: Depression and anxiety (seeing psychologist, challenging diagnosis and prognosis)
red_flags.action: Continue psychology support. Screen for depression/anxiety at each visit (PHQ-9, GAD-7 questionnaires). Discuss CFTR modulators' potential to improve quality of life and prognosis (may alleviate psychological burden). Consider antidepressant medication if symptoms severe.

learning_outcomes: Diagnose acute pulmonary exacerbation of cystic fibrosis using Fuchs criteria
Prescribe appropriate IV antibiotic therapy for Pseudomonas aeruginosa exacerbation (combination therapy, duration 14-21 days)
Understand CFTR modulator therapy (mechanism, eligibility, expected benefits, PBS criteria)
Discuss elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) with F508del homozygous patient
Coordinate multidisciplinary CF care (respiratory, physiotherapy, dietetics, endocrinology, psychology)
Optimize airway clearance, nutritional support, and pancreatic enzyme replacement
Manage CF-related complications: diabetes, liver disease, osteopenia, infertility
Recognize lung transplantation referral criteria and timing (FEV1 <30%, refractory disease)
Address psychosocial challenges in young adults with CF (employment, relationships, future planning)
Understand Australian CF specialist services and PBS access to CFTR modulators

key_tasks: Assess severity of acute pulmonary exacerbation (Fuchs criteria, FEV1 decline, systemic signs)
Prescribe appropriate IV antibiotic regimen for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (piperacillin/tazobactam + tobramycin, 14 days minimum)
Explain rationale for combination IV therapy (synergy, prevent resistance)
Discuss CFTR modulator eligibility (homozygous F508del, FEV1 38%, pancreatic insufficiency - meets PBS criteria)
Explain elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor mechanism, expected benefits, timeline for effect
Address nutritional optimization (high-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme adjustment, dietitian referral)
Optimize CFRD management (insulin adjustment during exacerbation, HbA1c target <7%)
Discuss airway clearance intensification during exacerbation (increase frequency to 3-4 sessions/day)

candidate_challenges: Integrating multiple complex CF-related issues (acute exacerbation, chronic complications, CFTR modulators, psychosocial)
Prioritizing immediate management (IV antibiotics, airway clearance, nutrition) while discussing long-term CFTR modulator therapy
Explaining complex CFTR modulator mechanism and PBS criteria in patient-friendly language
Balancing realistic prognosis discussion (severe disease, FEV1 <50%) with hope (CFTR modulators transformative)
Addressing multiple comorbidities (CFRD, liver disease, osteopenia) within 15-minute consultation
Demonstrating knowledge of Australian PBS criteria and specialist CF services
Communicating empathetically with young adult facing life-limiting disease
pass_criteria: Diagnoses acute CF pulmonary exacerbation, cites key features (increased symptoms, FEV1 decline, fever, CRP elevation, new CXR infiltrate)
Prescribes appropriate IV antibiotics: two anti-pseudomonal agents (e.g., piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly + tobramycin 10 mg/kg IV daily, levels-based dosing). Duration 14 days minimum.
Identifies patient as eligible for CFTR modulator therapy (homozygous F508del, FEV1 <90%, pancreatic insufficiency)
Explains elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor benefits: FEV1 improvement ~10-14%, reduced exacerbations ~50%, weight gain, QOL improvement
Discusses multidisciplinary management: physiotherapy (airway clearance), dietitian (nutrition, weight gain), endocrinology (CFRD optimization)
Addresses nutritional concerns (BMI 19.7, weight loss 3 kg, target BMI >22, high-calorie diet, optimize pancreatic enzymes)
Recognizes need for airway clearance intensification during exacerbation (3-4 sessions/day)
Discusses prognosis sensitively: FEV1 48% indicates severe disease, CFTR modulators may stabilize/improve lung function, potential to delay transplant
Addresses psychosocial support (psychology, depression/anxiety management, work adjustments, peer support groups)
common_errors: Prescribing single IV antibiotic instead of combination therapy (fails to provide synergy, allows resistance development)
Choosing oral antibiotics for severe exacerbation (inadequate for Pseudomonas aeruginosa in CF)
Not recognizing CFTR modulator eligibility (missing opportunity for disease-modifying therapy)
Overestimating or underestimating CFTR modulator benefits (realistic expectations: significant but not curative)
Failing to address multiple comorbidities (CFRD, liver disease, nutrition, bone health)
Not discussing lung transplantation (relevant for FEV1 <50%, patient should be aware of criteria)
Inadequate psychosocial assessment (missing depression, work challenges, relationship concerns)
Not coordinating multidisciplinary care (CF management requires team approach)

marking_criteria.criterion: Assesses acute pulmonary exacerbation severity and prescribes appropriate IV antibiotic therapy
marking_criteria.description: Diagnoses acute CF exacerbation (Fuchs criteria ≥4 features met). Prescribes combination IV antibiotics: piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly + tobramycin 10 mg/kg IV daily (levels-based dosing). Duration 14 days minimum. Explains rationale: synergy, prevent resistance, target Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Mentions monitoring: tobramycin levels (peak/trough), renal function, audiology.

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies CFTR modulator eligibility and discusses therapy
marking_criteria.description: Recognizes patient meets PBS criteria: homozygous F508del, FEV1 38% (<90%), pancreatic insufficiency, age ≥6 years. Recommends elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta). Explains mechanism: corrector + potentiator drugs improve CFTR protein function at cell membrane. Discusses initiation: requires specialist prescription, baseline LFTs, ophthalmology review (cataracts risk in children, not adults).

marking_criteria.criterion: Explains expected benefits and timeline of CFTR modulators
marking_criteria.description: Discusses realistic benefits: Absolute FEV1 increase 10-14 percentage points (patient's FEV1 may improve from 48% to 58-62%), 50-60% reduction in exacerbations, weight gain 2-4 kg, improved quality of life, sweat chloride normalization. Timeline: benefits within 4-12 weeks. Long-term: may stabilize disease, delay/prevent lung transplantation.

marking_criteria.criterion: Optimizes nutritional management
marking_criteria.description: Addresses weight loss (3 kg in 2 weeks, BMI 19.7 kg/m²). Refers to CF dietitian urgently. Recommends: high-calorie oral supplements, optimize pancreatic enzyme dose (may need to increase), target caloric intake 3,000-3,500 kcal/day. Target BMI >22 kg/m². Discusses potential for NG/PEG feeding if oral intake insufficient. Mentions CFTR modulators often improve appetite and weight gain.

marking_criteria.criterion: Manages CF-related diabetes appropriately
marking_criteria.description: Recognizes suboptimal control (HbA1c 7.8%, target <7%). Recommends: increase insulin doses during exacerbation (acute illness increases insulin resistance), frequent blood glucose monitoring (4-6x/day), carbohydrate counting review with diabetes educator. Optimize control before starting CFTR modulators. Long-term: dietitian input for weight gain without worsening diabetes.

marking_criteria.criterion: Intensifies airway clearance and respiratory support
marking_criteria.description: Recommends increased airway clearance frequency: 3-4 sessions/day during exacerbation (from usual 2/day). Continues nebulized hypertonic saline 7%, nebulized salbutamol before physiotherapy. Refers to physiotherapist for technique optimization. Continues oxygen therapy (currently 4 L/min, aim SpO2 ≥92%). Monitors for CO2 retention (consider ABG if clinical concern).

marking_criteria.criterion: Coordinates multidisciplinary CF care
marking_criteria.description: Plans multidisciplinary input: CF nurse specialist (adherence, education), physiotherapist (airway clearance), dietitian (nutrition optimization), endocrinology/diabetes educator (CFRD), psychologist (depression, anxiety, coping), social worker (disability support, employment). Schedules follow-up in CF clinic (2-4 weeks post-IV antibiotics to reassess FEV1 response).

marking_criteria.criterion: Discusses prognosis and lung transplantation
marking_criteria.description: Discusses prognosis honestly: FEV1 48% indicates severe lung disease, median survival for CF patients with FEV1 <30% is 2-3 years without transplant. CFTR modulators transformative: may stabilize lung function, reduce decline, delay/prevent transplantation. Mentions lung transplant as option if FEV1 continues to decline to <30% or refractory exacerbations. Balances realism with hope.

marking_criteria.criterion: Addresses psychosocial and lifestyle factors
marking_criteria.description: Explores impact on work, relationships, mental health. Validates concerns about future. Discusses depression/anxiety management (continue psychology, consider medication if needed). Fertility counselling: CBAVD (infertile), sperm retrieval + IVF option if desires children. Encourages peer support (CF Foundation, online CF communities, with infection control precautions). Discusses employment rights (disability discrimination protections).

marking_criteria.criterion: Communication skills and patient-centred approach
marking_criteria.description: Uses clear, jargon-free language when explaining CFTR modulators and management plan. Checks understanding frequently. Empathetic and supportive tone when discussing prognosis and challenges. Involves patient in treatment decisions (shared decision-making). Provides written information (CFTR modulator fact sheets, CF Foundation resources). Offers contact details for CF nurse specialist for questions.

marking_criteria.criterion: Professional behaviour and structure
marking_criteria.description: Professional demeanour. Structured approach: assesses exacerbation → immediate treatment (IV antibiotics) → discusses CFTR modulators → addresses comorbidities → psychosocial support. Efficient use of 15 minutes. Summarizes management plan clearly at end.
