osces.title: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis - Diagnosis and Treatment

patient_demographics.name: Rachel Thompson
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: worsening asthma with brown mucus plugs

osces.clinical_scenario: Ms Thompson presents to the respiratory clinic with a 6-month history of poorly controlled asthma despite high-dose ICS-LABA therapy. She reports coughing up brown, rubbery mucus plugs and experiencing recurrent chest infections. She has a history of moderate persistent asthma since childhood and allergic rhinitis. Recent chest X-ray shows fleeting upper lobe infiltrates.

presenting_complaint.main_symptom: worsening asthma control with expectoration of brown mucus plugs
presenting_complaint.character: thick, brown, rubbery sputum plugs, difficult to expectorate
presenting_complaint.exacerbating_factors: exposure to mould in classroom, humid weather
presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: temporary improvement with oral prednisolone courses
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness, fatigue, weight loss of 3kg

medical_history: 3 hospital admissions for asthma in past year
medications: fluticasone/formoterol 250/10 mcg 2 puffs BD (PBS code 10326F)
salbutamol MDI 100mcg PRN (PBS code 2178D)
montelukast 10mg nocte (PBS code 8254W)
loratadine 10mg daily (PBS code 2913Y)
prednisolone 25mg daily (current course day 5 of 7)
history_taking.allergies: house dust mites, Aspergillus fumigatus (skin prick test positive), grass pollen

social_history.alcohol: occasional social drinking
social_history.occupation: primary school teacher, old building with visible mould

history_taking.family_history: mother has asthma, father has eczema

physical_examination.general: young woman, mild respiratory distress, using accessory muscles, speaks in full sentences

respiratory.inspection: increased work of breathing, no cyanosis, no clubbing
respiratory.percussion: dull percussion note right upper zone
respiratory.auscultation: widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze, coarse crackles right upper lobe

physical_examination.cardiovascular: dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
physical_examination.other: nasal polyps visible on anterior rhinoscopy

initial.result: FEV1 1.8L (52% predicted), FVC 3.1L (75% predicted), FEV1/FVC 58%, post-bronchodilator FEV1 2.2L (64% predicted) - 22% improvement
Hb 128 g/L, WCC 12.3 x10^9/L, eosinophils 2.8 x10^9/L (23%), platelets 342 x10^9/L
2,840 IU/mL (normal <100 IU/mL)
48.2 kUA/L (positive >0.35 kUA/L)
142 mg/L (positive >40 mg/L)
right upper lobe consolidation with mucoid impaction, central bronchiectasis, previous left upper lobe infiltrate now resolved
central bronchiectasis, mucoid impaction in dilated bronchi ('finger-in-glove' sign), mosaic attenuation, right upper lobe consolidation
Aspergillus fumigatus isolated, sensitive to itraconazole and voriconazole

diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: meets ISHAM working group criteria: asthma, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, positive Aspergillus IgE and IgG, eosinophilia >500 cells/μL, radiological findings consistent with ABPA

immediate: continue current prednisolone 25mg daily
optimise asthma control with ICS-LABA
chest physiotherapy for mucus clearance
monitor oxygen saturation

pharmacological.dose: 0.5mg/kg/day (35mg) for 2 weeks, then taper over 3-6 months
pharmacological.monitoring: blood glucose, bone density if prolonged use
liver function tests monthly, drug levels, QTc monitoring

non_pharmacological: mould remediation at home and workplace
management.follow_up: respiratory clinic in 4 weeks with repeat IgE, eosinophil count, and chest X-ray

marking_criteria.criterion: identifies key features of ABPA presentation
appropriate history taking including occupational exposure
recognises significance of brown mucus plugs
orders appropriate investigations including Aspergillus serology
correctly interprets elevated IgE and eosinophilia
identifies central bronchiectasis on imaging
applies ISHAM diagnostic criteria correctly
initiates appropriate corticosteroid therapy
prescribes antifungal therapy with itraconazole
discusses monitoring requirements for itraconazole
addresses environmental mould exposure
arranges appropriate follow-up and monitoring
demonstrates safe prescribing with PBS authority requirements

osces.sample_answer: 28-year-old female teacher with poorly controlled asthma presenting with brown mucus plugs and recurrent infections. Examination reveals wheeze and right upper lobe crackles. Investigations show eosinophilia (2.8 x10^9/L), total IgE 2,840 IU/mL, positive Aspergillus IgE and IgG, and HRCT demonstrating central bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction. Diagnosis of ABPA confirmed using ISHAM criteria. Management includes prednisolone 35mg daily with gradual taper, itraconazole 200mg BD for 16 weeks (PBS authority 8470W), continued high-dose ICS-LABA, environmental mould remediation, and close monitoring of treatment response with serial IgE levels.

osces.title: Pneumocystis Pneumonia in HIV-Positive Patient

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Emergency Department
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath over 3 weeks, dry cough, and fever. He appears dyspnoeic at rest with oxygen saturations of 88% on room air.
scenario.background: Known HIV-positive (diagnosed 2019), poor compliance with antiretroviral therapy. Last CD4 count 6 months ago was 180 cells/μL. Works as a graphic designer, lives alone in Young. No recent travel. Non-smoker. No known drug allergies.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 88% on room air, 94% on 4L via nasal prongs

scenario.physical_examination: Patient appears cachectic (BMI 18.2). Mild oral candidiasis noted. Respiratory examination shows increased respiratory effort with accessory muscle use. No cyanosis. Chest expansion reduced bilaterally. Percussion resonant throughout. Auscultation reveals fine bibasal crackles, no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination normal. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. No skin lesions.

tasks: Obtain focused respiratory and HIV history including medication compliance
Assess severity of respiratory compromise and calculate CURB-65 score
Perform systematic respiratory examination
Interpret chest X-ray showing bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates
Order appropriate investigations including CD4 count, HIV viral load, ABG, sputum for PCP immunofluorescence
Initiate high-flow oxygen therapy targeting SpO2 92-96%
Prescribe empirical treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with co-trimoxazole and prednisolone
Assess criteria for ICU admission and escalation of care
Arrange urgent infectious diseases and HIV physician consultation
Counsel patient on importance of ART adherence and PCP prophylaxis
Document comprehensive management plan in medical record
Arrange hospital admission under respiratory medicine with isolation precautions
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in immunocompromised patients
Understand correlation between CD4 count and opportunistic infection risk (PCP typically occurs at CD4 <200)
Apply Australian guidelines for PCP treatment (eTG: co-trimoxazole 100mg/kg/day IV divided QID plus prednisolone if PaO2 <70mmHg)
Interpret arterial blood gas in context of respiratory failure and lactate dehydrogenase elevation
Calculate severity scores (CURB-65) and recognize need for HDU/ICU monitoring
Understand importance of corticosteroid therapy in moderate-to-severe PCP (reduces mortality)
Recognize need for urgent ART initiation coordination with infectious diseases team
Demonstrate culturally safe communication around HIV status and medication adherence
Arrange appropriate respiratory isolation for atypical pneumonia
Coordinate multidisciplinary care involving respiratory, infectious diseases, and HIV physicians
marking_criteria: Obtains comprehensive HIV history including CD4 trend, viral load, current ART regimen, and compliance barriers
Performs systematic respiratory examination including oxygen requirement assessment and work of breathing
Correctly interprets bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates on CXR as consistent with PCP
Orders CD4 count, HIV viral load, LDH (typically >500 U/L in PCP), beta-D-glucan, ABG, and induced sputum for PCP immunofluorescence
Initiates appropriate oxygen therapy targeting SpO2 92-96% (aware of risks of hyperoxia in HIV patients)
Prescribes co-trimoxazole 1680mg IV QID (trimethoprim 15-20mg/kg/day component) for 21 days
Prescribes prednisolone 40mg BD for 5 days, then 40mg daily for 5 days, then 20mg daily for 11 days (total 21 days) if PaO2 <70mmHg or A-a gradient >35mmHg
Recognizes severe respiratory failure requiring HDU/ICU admission (RR >30, SpO2 <90% on high-flow oxygen, confusion)
Arranges urgent infectious diseases consultation for ART optimization and PCP prophylaxis planning
Counsels patient sensitively about medication adherence using non-judgmental approach and exploring barriers
Documents comprehensive assessment including HIV status, CD4 count, treatment plan, and infection control precautions
Arranges hospital admission with respiratory isolation until bacterial pneumonia excluded and considers TB screening
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests recognition of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in the context of HIV immunosuppression. Key assessment points: (1) Correlation of CD4 count with opportunistic infection risk, (2) Interpretation of typical CXR findings (bilateral interstitial infiltrates vs normal in 10-20% of cases), (3) Use of adjunctive corticosteroids based on PaO2 criteria (reduces mortality in moderate-to-severe PCP), (4) Understanding that LDH is typically elevated (>500 U/L) and can guide severity, (5) Recognition of need for 21-day treatment course (longer than bacterial pneumonia). Common errors: failing to prescribe corticosteroids in severe PCP, using trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole dosing appropriate for UTI rather than PCP, not recognizing need for ART optimization, inadequate oxygen therapy. Australian context: PBS authority required for co-trimoxazole at high doses (streamlined authority code 4677), coordination with state HIV services, notification requirements. Candidates should demonstrate non-judgmental communication around HIV and medication adherence.
osces.model_answer_summary: This 42-year-old man with poorly controlled HIV (CD4 180) presents with classic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: subacute dyspnoea (3 weeks), dry cough, fever, and hypoxia with bilateral interstitial infiltrates. CD4 <200 increases PCP risk 100-fold. Immediate management: high-flow oxygen targeting 92-96%, co-trimoxazole 1680mg IV QID for 21 days, prednisolone 40mg BD (PaO2 likely <70mmHg given SpO2 88% on air). Investigations: ABG (expected Type 1 respiratory failure, A-a gradient >35mmHg), CD4 count, HIV viral load, LDH (expect >500 U/L), induced sputum for PCP immunofluorescence (diagnostic yield 55-90%), beta-D-glucan (sensitivity 95%). CURB-65 score 1-2 suggests severe pneumonia. HDU admission for close respiratory monitoring. Urgent infectious diseases consultation for ART optimization (timing controversial but usually within 2 weeks once PCP treatment started). After discharge: lifelong PCP prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole 960mg daily if CD4 remains <200. Patient education on ART adherence critical to immune reconstitution. Prognosis: mortality 10-20% with treatment, 100% without. Close monitoring for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) once ART commenced.
references: eTG Complete - Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment protocol (co-trimoxazole 100mg/kg/day divided QID)
Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine (ASHM) - PCP prophylaxis guidelines
Thomas CF, Limper AH. Pneumocystis pneumonia. N Engl J Med 2004;350:2487-98
PBS Schedule - Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim 160mg + sulfamethoxazole 800mg) tablets and IV - Authority required for high-dose PCP treatment
Australian HIV Observational Database - Opportunistic infection trends and CD4 thresholds
NSW Health HIV Management Guidelines - ART initiation timing in acute opportunistic infections

osces.title: Empyema - Chest Drain Management and Surgical Referral

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Medical Ward
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 58-year-old woman with ongoing fever and pleuritic chest pain despite 5 days of IV antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia. Chest drain inserted 24 hours ago draining thick purulent fluid.
scenario.background: Presented 6 days ago with right lower lobe pneumonia, treated with IV benzylpenicillin and azithromycin. Persistent fever and pleural effusion on repeat CXR led to diagnostic thoracentesis showing pH 6.95, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, LDH 1450 U/L, and purulent appearance. Chest drain (24Fr) inserted yesterday draining 400mL thick yellow-green fluid initially, now draining 20mL/hour. Past history: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%), ex-smoker (30 pack-years, quit 2017). Lives on farm outside Young. Allergic to penicillin (rash).
scenario.physical_examination: Patient appears unwell and febrile. Chest drain in situ in right 5th intercostal space mid-axillary line, draining small amounts of thick purulent fluid. Respiratory examination: reduced expansion right lower chest, dull to percussion right base extending to mid-zone, reduced breath sounds and bronchial breathing right lower zone, no pleural rub. Cardiovascular examination normal. No peripheral oedema. Surgical emphysema not present around drain site.

tasks: Review chest drain function and confirm correct positioning on chest X-ray
Assess pleural fluid characteristics and interpret biochemical analysis indicating complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema
Review microbiology results from pleural fluid culture and adjust antibiotic therapy accordingly
Recognize features indicating need for surgical intervention (loculated collection, thick pus, failed medical drainage)
Arrange urgent CT chest with contrast to assess for loculations and lung abscess
Optimize chest drain management including flushing protocol and suction settings
Escalate antibiotic therapy to cover Streptococcus anginosus group and anaerobes with moxifloxacin and metronidazole
Arrange urgent cardiothoracic surgical consultation for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)
Manage diabetes during acute infection with insulin sliding scale
Provide analgesia for pleuritic chest pain enabling effective cough and deep breathing
Discuss treatment options with patient including need for possible surgical intervention
Arrange transfer to tertiary hospital with cardiothoracic surgical services if VATS required
learning_objectives: Recognize complicated parapneumonic effusion progressing to empyema based on Light's criteria and pleural fluid characteristics
Interpret pleural fluid analysis: empyema defined by pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000 U/L, or frank pus
Understand three stages of empyema: exudative (thin fluid), fibrinopurulent (thick fluid, loculations), organizing (fibrosis)
Apply Australian guidelines for chest drain management in empyema (British Thoracic Society adapted for Australia)
Recognize indications for surgical referral: loculations on imaging, thick pus, failed drainage after 3-5 days, ongoing sepsis
Understand role of VATS vs open decortication in empyema management (VATS preferred if suitable anatomy)
Prescribe appropriate antibiotics for empyema covering Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and anaerobes
Manage chest drain complications including blockage, dislodgement, and surgical emphysema
Coordinate care between rural hospital and tertiary cardiothoracic surgical unit for transfer
Understand importance of adequate analgesia to prevent restrictive lung disease from chronic empyema
marking_criteria: Reviews chest X-ray confirming drain position in pleural space and assessing for residual collection or loculations
Correctly interprets pleural fluid analysis showing empyema: pH 6.95 (<7.2), glucose 1.8 (<2.2), LDH 1450 (>1000), purulent appearance
Recognizes thick purulent fluid and poor drainage (20mL/hr) as indicators of fibrinopurulent stage requiring surgical intervention
Orders urgent CT chest with IV contrast to assess extent of empyema, presence of loculations, and exclude lung abscess
Optimizes chest drain management: ensures drain patent (flush with 20mL sterile saline if blocked), applies low-pressure suction (-10 to -20 cmH2O)
Changes antibiotic therapy from penicillin to moxifloxacin 400mg IV daily (covers Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypicals, safe in penicillin allergy)
Adds metronidazole 500mg IV TDS to cover anaerobes (aspiration risk in diabetic patient with possible reduced consciousness)
Arranges urgent cardiothoracic surgical consultation within 24 hours for VATS debridement and decortication
Manages hyperglycaemia with insulin sliding scale (target 6-10 mmol/L during acute infection, poorly controlled diabetes impairs immune function)
Prescribes adequate analgesia: regular paracetamol 1g QID plus oxycodone 5-10mg Q4H PRN (enabling deep breathing and cough)
Explains need for surgical intervention to patient: likely VATS procedure, small incisions, drainage of pus, breaking down loculations, average 3-5 day hospital stay post-VATS
Coordinates transfer to tertiary centre (Wagga Wagga Base Hospital or Canberra Hospital) with cardiothoracic surgical services, ensuring patient stability for road transfer (2-3 hours)
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests management of complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema requiring surgical intervention. Key assessment points: (1) Interpretation of pleural fluid analysis showing empyema (pH <7.2 is critical threshold), (2) Recognition that thick purulent fluid with poor drainage indicates fibrinopurulent stage unlikely to respond to antibiotics and drainage alone, (3) Understanding VATS timing (early intervention within 7 days improves outcomes vs late decortication), (4) Appropriate antibiotic escalation in penicillin-allergic patient (moxifloxacin covers resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae), (5) Rural context requiring transfer to tertiary centre. Common errors: continuing medical management when surgical referral indicated, inadequate analgesia leading to restrictive defect, failing to recognize loculations on imaging, inappropriate antibiotic choice in penicillin allergy. Australian context: Rural hospital limitations requiring tertiary transfer, coordination with RFDS if patient deteriorates and needs air retrieval, PBS coverage for moxifloxacin requires authority for empyema (streamlined code 4283). Candidates should demonstrate clear communication about need for surgery and transfer.
osces.model_answer_summary: This 58-year-old woman has empyema complicating community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), indicated by pleural fluid pH 6.95, glucose 1.8, LDH 1450, and purulent appearance. Failed response to antibiotics and chest drainage (persistent fever, poor drain output 20mL/hr) suggests fibrinopurulent stage with loculations requiring surgical intervention. Immediate management: (1) CT chest confirms loculations and excludes lung abscess, (2) Optimize chest drain: flush with 20mL sterile saline to clear thick pus, apply low-pressure suction -20cmH2O, (3) Escalate antibiotics (penicillin allergy): moxifloxacin 400mg IV daily + metronidazole 500mg IV TDS covering Streptococcus, anaerobes, and resistant organisms, (4) Urgent cardiothoracic surgery referral for VATS within 24-48 hours (early intervention improves outcomes), (5) Analgesia: paracetamol 1g QID + oxycodone 5-10mg Q4H PRN (inadequate pain control leads to shallow breathing and restrictive defect), (6) Insulin sliding scale for diabetes (HbA1c 8.2% indicates poor control, infection worsens hyperglycaemia). VATS procedure involves debridement, drainage, breaking down loculations, and decortication if fibrous peel present. Success rate 85-95% if performed early. If VATS fails or anatomy unsuitable, open thoracotomy and decortication required. Transfer to Wagga Wagga Base Hospital or Canberra Hospital for cardiothoracic surgery. Prognosis: mortality 5-15% with appropriate treatment, higher if delayed intervention or organizing stage reached. Post-operative: chest drains remain 3-7 days until output <150mL/day and lung re-expanded.
references: eTG Complete - Empyema management and antibiotic selection (moxifloxacin for penicillin allergy)
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) - Pleural disease guidelines
Davies HE, et al. Management of pleural infection in adults: British Thoracic Society pleural disease guideline 2010. Thorax 2010;65:ii41-53
Light RW. Pleural effusions. Med Clin North Am 2011;95:1055-70 (Light's criteria for exudates)
PBS Schedule - Moxifloxacin 400mg tablets/IV - Authority required (streamlined) for complicated parapneumonic effusion
Australian and New Zealand Journal of Surgery - VATS vs open decortication outcomes in empyema

osces.title: Aspiration Pneumonia - Swallowing Assessment and Antibiotics

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Emergency Department
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 76-year-old man from an aged care facility presents with fever, cough, and confusion over 24 hours. Nursing staff report he had a choking episode during lunch yesterday.
scenario.background: Nursing home resident with advanced dementia (MMSE 12/30), previous stroke 2021 with residual right-sided weakness. Known dysphagia managed with thickened fluids and pureed diet. Yesterday witnessed choking on normal-consistency soup, coughed for several minutes then seemed to settle. Overnight developed fever and increased confusion. Medications: aspirin 100mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg nocte, donepezil 10mg daily, thickened fluids. No known allergies. Next of kin: daughter (lives in Canberra, has medical power of attorney).

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 91% on room air, 96% on 3L via nasal prongs

scenario.physical_examination: Elderly man, confused and drowsy, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Mild dehydration (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor). Respiratory examination: increased work of breathing, coarse crepitations right lower zone, bronchial breathing right base. Cardiovascular examination normal. Neurological examination: right-sided weakness (4/5 power), increased tone right arm and leg, brisk reflexes right side, equivocal plantar responses. Cough reflex weak. Oral examination: poor dentition, food debris in mouth, no obvious oral candidiasis.

tasks: Obtain collateral history from nursing home staff regarding choking episode and baseline swallowing function
Perform focused respiratory and neurological examination including assessment of cough and gag reflex
Recognize clinical features of aspiration pneumonia: witnessed aspiration, right lower lobe infiltrate, at-risk patient population
Interpret chest X-ray showing right lower lobe consolidation consistent with aspiration
Order appropriate investigations including blood cultures, sputum culture, FBC, UEC, and inflammatory markers
Assess swallowing safety using bedside swallow screen (water swallow test contraindicated until infection treated)
Prescribe antibiotics covering aspiration pneumonia organisms including anaerobes (amoxicillin-clavulanate plus metronidazole)
Initiate nil-by-mouth status pending formal speech pathology swallowing assessment
Arrange IV fluids for hydration and nutrition support planning
Contact daughter (next of kin) to discuss diagnosis, treatment plan, and goals of care in context of advanced dementia
Arrange hospital admission under geriatric medicine with speech pathology and dietitian referrals
Document advanced care planning discussion and resuscitation status
learning_objectives: Recognize risk factors for aspiration pneumonia: dysphagia (stroke, dementia, neuromuscular disease), impaired consciousness, poor dentition
Understand microbiology of aspiration pneumonia: mixed oral flora including Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium)
Apply Australian guidelines for antibiotic selection in aspiration pneumonia (eTG: amoxicillin-clavulanate covers typical CAP organisms plus anaerobes)
Perform bedside swallowing assessment and recognize when formal speech pathology evaluation required
Understand principles of dysphagia management: diet modification (IDDSI levels), positioning, oral hygiene
Recognize aspiration pneumonia as sentinel event requiring swallowing assessment before oral intake resumed
Coordinate multidisciplinary care involving geriatrics, speech pathology, dietitian, and palliative care
Demonstrate culturally safe communication with family regarding prognosis and goals of care in advanced dementia
Understand role of advance care directives and medical power of attorney in treatment decisions
Consider prevention strategies: oral hygiene, positioning during meals, medication review (anticholinergics worsen dysphagia)
marking_criteria: Obtains detailed collateral history from nursing home including witnessed choking episode, baseline diet consistency (IDDSI level 4 pureed diet), and previous swallowing assessments
Performs systematic respiratory examination identifying right lower lobe signs (consolidation in dependent lung segment typical for aspiration)
Assesses neurological function including cough reflex (weak suggests impaired airway protection) and gag reflex
Correctly interprets CXR showing right lower lobe consolidation (aspiration typically affects dependent segments: right lower lobe or posterior segments upper lobes if supine)

Orders appropriate investigations: blood cultures x2 (before antibiotics), sputum culture (often polymicrobial), FBC (WCC likely elevated), CRP (elevated), UEC (assess renal function for antibiotic dosing)
Prescribes amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g IV TDS (covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, oral anaerobes) plus metronidazole 500mg IV TDS (additional anaerobic cover)
Implements nil-by-mouth (NBM) status immediately and documents clearly in medication chart and nursing notes
Orders IV fluids (e.g., 0.9% sodium chloride 1L over 8 hours) for hydration, recognizing enteral feeding route needed if dysphagia persists
Refers to speech pathology urgently for bedside swallow screen when infection treated, followed by videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) if screen abnormal

Contacts daughter (medical power of attorney) within 4 hours of admission to discuss diagnosis, likely prolonged recovery, and goals of care in context of advanced dementia (average survival 1-2 years)

Documents advance care planning discussion including resuscitation status (likely not for CPR given advanced dementia and poor functional baseline), ceiling of treatment, and patient/family preferences
Arranges admission under geriatric medicine (expertise in frailty, dementia, and dysphagia management) with allied health referrals (speech pathology, dietitian, occupational therapy for positioning)
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests recognition and management of aspiration pneumonia in an elderly patient with dementia and dysphagia. Key assessment points: (1) Recognition of witnessed aspiration as key historical feature, (2) Understanding that aspiration pneumonia affects dependent lung segments (right lower lobe if upright, posterior segments if supine), (3) Importance of anaerobic antibiotic coverage (oral flora includes anaerobes), (4) Immediate NBM status to prevent further aspiration, (5) Role of speech pathology in swallowing assessment. Common errors: using antibiotics for typical CAP without anaerobic coverage (e.g., benzylpenicillin alone), allowing oral intake before swallowing assessment, failing to involve speech pathology, inadequate discussion of goals of care with family. Australian context: IDDSI (International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative) framework used for diet modification, PBS coverage for PEG tube feeding supplies if long-term enteral nutrition required, aged care standards requiring swallowing screening. Candidates should demonstrate sensitivity in goals-of-care discussions recognizing poor prognosis in advanced dementia with aspiration pneumonia (6-month mortality 40-50%).
osces.model_answer_summary: This 76-year-old nursing home resident with advanced dementia, previous stroke, and known dysphagia presents with aspiration pneumonia following witnessed choking episode. Clinical features consistent with aspiration: (1) Witnessed aspiration event, (2) Right lower lobe consolidation (dependent segment), (3) At-risk population (dysphagia, impaired consciousness), (4) Acute deterioration post-aspiration. Immediate management: (1) NBM status (critical to prevent further aspiration), (2) Antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g IV TDS + metronidazole 500mg IV TDS for 5-7 days (covers oral anaerobes including Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus), (3) IV hydration: 0.9% NaCl 1L/8hr (assess renal function first), (4) Oxygen therapy 3L to maintain SpO2 >92%, (5) Urgent speech pathology referral for bedside swallow screen when clinically improved (typically day 3-5), followed by VFSS if abnormal. Risk factors: stroke-related dysphagia, dementia (reduced awareness of aspiration), poor dentition (increased bacterial load). Goals of care discussion with daughter (MPOA): Explain aspiration pneumonia diagnosis, likely need for enteral feeding (NGT short-term or PEG if dysphagia persists >4 weeks), prognosis in advanced dementia (6-month mortality 40-50% post-aspiration pneumonia), clarify resuscitation status (likely NFR given baseline MMSE 12 and poor functional status). Prevention strategies if recovers: strict adherence to thickened fluids (IDDSI level 2), pureed diet (IDDSI level 4), upright positioning 30-45 minutes post-meals, oral hygiene (reduce bacterial load), medication review (avoid anticholinergics that worsen dysphagia). Admission under geriatric medicine for frailty and dementia expertise.
references: eTG Complete - Community-acquired pneumonia including aspiration pneumonia (amoxicillin-clavulanate + metronidazole regimen)
Therapeutic Guidelines - Aspiration pneumonia antibiotic selection covering anaerobes
IDDSI Framework - International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative levels for diet modification
Marik PE. Aspiration pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia. N Engl J Med 2001;344:665-71
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care - Dysphagia screening in hospitals
Speech Pathology Australia - Clinical guideline for videofluoroscopic swallow study

osces.title: Sarcoidosis - Diagnostic Workup and Steroid Therapy

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Respiratory Clinic
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 34-year-old woman referred by GP with 3-month history of dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, and bilateral ankle swelling. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
scenario.background: Primary school teacher, previously well. Three months ago developed dry cough and noticed reduced exercise tolerance (previously ran 5km three times weekly, now dyspnoeic after 1km). Also notes painful red lumps on shins over past 4 weeks. No weight loss, fever, or night sweats. No recent overseas travel. Non-smoker, no alcohol or recreational drugs. Family history: cousin with Crohn's disease. Born in Australia, parents immigrated from Greece in 1980s. No known drug allergies.
scenario.physical_examination: Young woman, appears well. Skin examination: bilateral tender erythematous nodules on anterior shins (erythema nodosum). Respiratory examination: chest expansion symmetrical, percussion resonant throughout, auscultation reveals fine end-inspiratory crackles at lung bases bilaterally, no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination normal. Peripheral examination: mild bilateral ankle swelling (non-pitting), no calf tenderness. Eye examination: no uveitis or conjunctival injection visible. Lymph nodes: no palpable cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. No hepatosplenomegaly.

tasks: Obtain detailed history focusing on systemic symptoms of sarcoidosis (cough, dyspnoea, constitutional symptoms)
Perform systematic respiratory examination and assess for extrapulmonary manifestations of sarcoidosis
Review chest X-ray showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and classify according to Scadding staging
Order comprehensive investigations including spirometry, HRCT chest, serum ACE level, calcium, and inflammatory markers
Arrange tissue diagnosis via endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) or mediastinoscopy
Assess for extrapulmonary involvement: ophthalmology review (uveitis), ECG and echocardiogram (cardiac sarcoidosis), 24-hour urine calcium
Interpret pulmonary function tests showing restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO
Determine need for corticosteroid therapy based on symptoms, pulmonary function, and staging
Prescribe prednisolone with appropriate initial dose, tapering schedule, and monitoring plan
Educate patient on sarcoidosis natural history, treatment duration (typically 12-24 months), and monitoring requirements
Arrange specialist respiratory physician follow-up and multidisciplinary care coordination
Discuss prognosis including likelihood of spontaneous remission vs chronic disease
learning_objectives: Recognize classic presentation of Löfgren syndrome: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and arthralgia (excellent prognosis, often self-limiting)

Apply Scadding staging system for pulmonary sarcoidosis (Stage I: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy alone, Stage II: hilar lymphadenopathy + parenchymal infiltrates, Stage III: parenchymal infiltrates alone, Stage IV: pulmonary fibrosis)
Understand diagnostic approach to sarcoidosis: exclusion of other granulomatous diseases, histological confirmation of non-caseating granulomas
Interpret serum ACE level (elevated in 60% of active sarcoidosis, useful for monitoring disease activity but not diagnostic)
Recognize indications for systemic corticosteroid therapy: symptomatic disease, declining lung function, cardiac or neurological involvement, hypercalcaemia
Apply Australian guidelines for corticosteroid dosing in sarcoidosis (prednisolone 0.5mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks, then taper over 12 months minimum)
Understand importance of screening for extrapulmonary sarcoidosis: eyes (uveitis 25-30%), heart (arrhythmias, heart block 5%), kidneys (hypercalcaemia 10%), nervous system (cranial nerve palsies 5%)
Recognize hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis due to extra-renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granulomas converting vitamin D to active form
Coordinate multidisciplinary care involving respiratory medicine, ophthalmology, cardiology, and rheumatology
Understand prognosis: Löfgren syndrome has 85-90% spontaneous remission rate, chronic disease occurs in 10-30% overall
marking_criteria: Elicits classic Löfgren syndrome triad: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (on CXR), erythema nodosum (bilateral shin lesions), and arthralgia (ankle swelling)
Performs comprehensive respiratory examination identifying fine bibasal crackles (suggests Stage II disease with parenchymal involvement)
Correctly classifies chest X-ray as Scadding Stage I or II (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, assess for parenchymal infiltrates)

Orders appropriate investigations: HRCT chest (assess parenchymal involvement and guide biopsy), spirometry and DLCO (restrictive pattern with reduced diffusion capacity), serum ACE (elevated in 60%), serum calcium (hypercalcaemia in 10%), 24-hour urine calcium (hypercalciuria more common than hypercalcaemia)
Arranges tissue diagnosis via EBUS-TBNA (first-line, diagnostic yield 80-90%, confirms non-caseating granulomas, excludes lymphoma and TB)

Orders screening for extrapulmonary involvement: ECG (arrhythmias, heart block), echocardiogram if cardiac symptoms, ophthalmology review (slit-lamp examination for uveitis), tuberculin skin test (often anergic in sarcoidosis)
Interprets pulmonary function tests: FVC and TLC reduced (restrictive pattern), FEV1/FVC ratio normal or increased, DLCO significantly reduced (impaired gas exchange)
Recognizes Löfgren syndrome as variant with excellent prognosis (85-90% spontaneous remission) but still warrants treatment if symptomatic
Prescribes prednisolone 0.5mg/kg/day (approximately 30-40mg daily for 70kg patient) for 4-6 weeks initial phase, then taper by 5mg every 4 weeks over 12 months minimum

Implements corticosteroid monitoring plan: bone protection (calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonate if age >50 or prior fracture), glucose monitoring (diabetes risk), PPI for gastric protection, ophthalmology review 3-monthly for steroid-induced glaucoma

Provides patient education: sarcoidosis is multisystem granulomatous disease, Löfgren syndrome has good prognosis, treatment typically 12-24 months, regular monitoring with spirometry and CXR every 3-6 months, risk of relapse 20-30% after stopping treatment

Arranges specialist respiratory physician referral for ongoing management and consideration of steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine) if prolonged treatment required or steroid intolerance
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests recognition of Löfgren syndrome, a distinct variant of sarcoidosis with excellent prognosis, and appropriate diagnostic workup for sarcoidosis. Key assessment points: (1) Recognition of classic Löfgren triad (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, arthralgia), (2) Understanding that Scadding Stage I-II disease has better prognosis than Stage III-IV, (3) Need for tissue diagnosis to exclude lymphoma and tuberculosis (EBUS-TBNA preferred over mediastinoscopy), (4) Appropriate corticosteroid dosing and tapering schedule (too-rapid taper causes relapse), (5) Monitoring for extrapulmonary involvement especially cardiac (can cause sudden death). Common errors: starting corticosteroids without tissue diagnosis (risk missing lymphoma or TB), inadequate monitoring for corticosteroid side effects, failing to screen for cardiac involvement, using serum ACE as diagnostic test (only 60% sensitive). Australian context: EBUS-TBNA available at tertiary centres (requires referral from Young Hospital), PBS requires authority for methotrexate as steroid-sparing agent in sarcoidosis, coordination with specialist respiratory physician (nearest at Wagga Wagga or Canberra). Candidates should explain that Löfgren syndrome often self-limiting but treatment improves symptoms and prevents progression.
osces.model_answer_summary: This 34-year-old woman presents with Löfgren syndrome, a distinct sarcoidosis variant with excellent prognosis: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + erythema nodosum + ankle arthralgia. Diagnosis requires tissue confirmation (exclude lymphoma, TB): EBUS-TBNA showing non-caseating granulomas without acid-fast bacilli. Investigations: (1) HRCT chest confirms bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, assess parenchymal involvement (Stage I vs II), (2) Pulmonary function tests show restrictive pattern (FVC 70% predicted, TLC 75% predicted, FEV1/FVC 82% - normal ratio, DLCO 65% predicted - reduced diffusion), (3) Serum ACE elevated (75 U/L, normal <40), (4) Serum calcium normal or mildly elevated (monitor for hypercalcaemia), 24-hour urine calcium elevated (hypercalciuria 40%), (5) ECG and echocardiogram normal (cardiac sarcoidosis in 5%, can cause heart block or arrhythmias), (6) Ophthalmology review excludes uveitis (present in 25-30%). Treatment decision: Despite good prognosis of Löfgren syndrome (85-90% spontaneous remission), symptomatic disease (dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance) and reduced DLCO warrant corticosteroid therapy. Prednisolone 30mg daily (0.5mg/kg for 60kg patient) for 6 weeks, then taper by 5mg every 4-6 weeks over 12-18 months minimum. Monitoring: spirometry and CXR every 3 months, serum ACE every 3 months (trend more useful than absolute value), bone protection (calcium 600mg + vitamin D 1000IU daily, DEXA scan at baseline and 12 months), diabetes screening (HbA1c 3-monthly), PPI (esomeprazole 20mg daily), ophthalmology 3-6 monthly. Prognosis: 85-90% achieve remission with treatment, relapse rate 20-30% after stopping corticosteroids, chronic disease requiring long-term immunosuppression occurs in 10-15%. Alternative agents if steroid intolerance or prolonged disease: methotrexate 10-15mg weekly (steroid-sparing), hydroxychloroquine 200mg BD (especially if skin or hypercalcaemia). Follow-up: respiratory physician 3-monthly during treatment, then 6-monthly for 2 years post-treatment.
references: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) - Sarcoidosis diagnostic and management guidelines

Statement on sarcoidosis. Joint Statement of the American Thoracic Society (ATS), the European Respiratory Society (ERS) and the World Association of Sarcoidosis and Other Granulomatous Disorders (WASOG). Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1999;160:736-55
Crouser ED, et al. Diagnosis and detection of sarcoidosis. An official American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2020;201:e26-51
eTG Complete - Sarcoidosis treatment with corticosteroids (prednisolone dosing and monitoring)
PBS Schedule - Prednisolone tablets (authority required for doses >25mg daily for >3 months)
Scadding JG. Prognosis of intrathoracic sarcoidosis in England. Br Med J 1961;2:1165-72 (Scadding staging system)

osces.title: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis - Oxygen Therapy and Palliative Care

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Outpatient Respiratory Clinic
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 68-year-old man with known idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis presents for routine follow-up. Progressive dyspnoea on exertion over past 3 months, now breathless walking 20 metres. Resting oxygen saturations 88% on room air, dropping to 78% on 6-minute walk test.
scenario.background: Diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) 18 months ago via HRCT and multidisciplinary team discussion (no lung biopsy performed - typical UIP pattern on CT). Currently on pirfenidone 801mg TDS. Ex-farmer (45 years exposure to grain dust, hay), ex-smoker (40 pack-year history, quit at diagnosis). Baseline FVC at diagnosis was 68% predicted, recent spirometry shows FVC 52% predicted (decline >10% in 6 months). DLCO 38% predicted. Lives with wife on farm 30km from Young. Previous gastro-oesophageal reflux managed with pantoprazole. No known drug allergies.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 88% on room air, 94% on 2L via nasal prongs

scenario.physical_examination: Elderly man, respiratory distress evident at rest. Clubbing present bilateral fingers. Respiratory examination: reduced chest expansion, percussion resonant, fine late-inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields ('Velcro crackles'), no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination: loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension), no murmurs, elevated JVP at 6cm, mild bilateral ankle oedema. No cyanosis at rest on supplemental oxygen. Weight 74kg (lost 8kg over past 6 months).

tasks: Review disease progression based on pulmonary function trends (FVC decline >10% indicates disease progression)
Assess oxygen requirements using 6-minute walk test with oximetry monitoring
Prescribe long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) according to Australian guidelines (SpO2 ≤88% at rest or exercise desaturation)
Review current antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone) and assess for side effects and efficacy
Assess for complications of IPF including pulmonary hypertension (loud P2, JVP elevation, ankle oedema) and arrange echocardiogram
Screen for lung cancer (increased risk in IPF, especially ex-smokers)
Initiate palliative care referral and discuss prognosis (median survival 3-5 years from diagnosis, patient now 18 months post-diagnosis with rapid progression)
Introduce advance care planning discussion including resuscitation status and preferred place of care
Assess suitability for lung transplant referral (age <65 preferred, this patient 68 but otherwise suitable)
Provide symptomatic management for dyspnoea including opioids for refractory breathlessness
Organize home oxygen equipment and patient education on oxygen use, flow rates, safety
Arrange multidisciplinary team follow-up including respiratory physician, palliative care, occupational therapy for mobility aids
learning_objectives: Recognize criteria for disease progression in IPF: FVC decline >10% in 6 months, worsening dyspnoea, declining exercise capacity
Apply Australian guidelines for long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT): indicated if SpO2 ≤88% at rest or exercise desaturation to ≤88%
Understand role of antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) in slowing FVC decline (reduces rate by ~50% but does not reverse fibrosis)
Recognize complications of IPF: pulmonary hypertension (30-40% of patients), lung cancer (7-fold increased risk), acute exacerbations
Understand prognosis of IPF: median survival 3-5 years from diagnosis, worse if rapid FVC decline, older age, or extensive fibrosis on HRCT
Apply lung transplant referral criteria: age <65 (relative), FVC <80% predicted, DLCO <40% predicted, absence of significant comorbidities
Demonstrate palliative care approach to dyspnoea management: oxygen therapy, opioids (morphine 2.5mg PO PRN reduces sensation of breathlessness), anxiolytics if anxiety
Facilitate advance care planning discussions sensitively, exploring patient values and preferences for end-of-life care
Understand oxygen delivery systems: continuous flow vs pulse-dose, stationary concentrators vs portable cylinders, flow rate titration
Coordinate home-based care involving respiratory physician, palliative care, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and community nursing
marking_criteria: Reviews pulmonary function trends identifying significant disease progression: FVC declined from 68% to 52% predicted (>10% absolute decline over 6 months indicates poor prognosis)
Correctly interprets 6-minute walk test showing exercise desaturation (SpO2 78%) meeting criteria for long-term oxygen therapy
Prescribes LTOT according to Australian Thoracic Society guidelines: oxygen 2-3L/min via nasal prongs targeting SpO2 90-92%, use minimum 15 hours/day including sleep
Reviews pirfenidone therapy assessing efficacy (slowing but not stopping FVC decline acceptable) and side effects (photosensitivity, nausea, rash)
Recognizes clinical features of pulmonary hypertension (loud P2, elevated JVP, ankle oedema) and orders echocardiogram to assess RV systolic pressure (RVSP >40mmHg suggests pulmonary hypertension)
Orders chest CT to screen for lung cancer (7-fold increased risk in IPF, symptoms of weight loss concerning)
Initiates early palliative care referral (evidence shows improved quality of life and reduced hospital admissions in IPF when palliative care involved early)

Conducts advance care planning discussion exploring resuscitation wishes (IPF patients rarely survive CPR - survival <1%), preferred place of death (home vs hospital), and goals of care (comfort vs life-prolonging interventions)

Assesses lung transplant suitability: Age 68 is borderline (upper limit traditionally 65, some centres accept up to 70), FVC 52% and DLCO 38% meet criteria, discusses with patient and refers to transplant centre (St Vincent's Hospital Sydney or The Alfred Melbourne)
Prescribes symptomatic dyspnoea management: morphine 2.5mg PO Q4H PRN (reduces dyspnoea sensation via central mechanism), lorazepam 0.5mg PO PRN if anxiety exacerbating breathlessness

Organizes home oxygen setup: oxygen concentrator for home use, portable oxygen cylinders for mobility (4-hour duration at 2L/min), patient and carer education on flow rate adjustment (increase to 4L/min during exertion), fire safety (no smoking, oxygen away from open flames)

Arranges comprehensive follow-up: respiratory physician 4-weekly (monitor disease progression), palliative care 2-weekly (symptom management), occupational therapy home assessment (mobility aids, energy conservation techniques), pulmonary rehabilitation if tolerated (improves exercise capacity and quality of life despite no change in lung function)
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests management of advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with focus on oxygen therapy, palliative care, and advance care planning. Key assessment points: (1) Recognition of disease progression based on FVC decline >10% (strong predictor of mortality), (2) Appropriate prescription of LTOT meeting Australian guidelines (SpO2 ≤88% at rest or exercise), (3) Early palliative care involvement (evidence-based in IPF to improve quality of life), (4) Sensitive advance care planning discussion (median survival 3-5 years, patient already 18 months from diagnosis with rapid progression suggests limited life expectancy), (5) Lung transplant assessment (age borderline but rapid progression warrants discussion). Common errors: waiting for severe hypoxia before prescribing oxygen (earlier initiation improves quality of life), not recognizing pulmonary hypertension as complication (present in 30-40% of IPF patients), avoiding prognostic discussions (patients want to know prognosis to plan), continuing antifibrotic therapy without assessing efficacy (if FVC declining >10% per year, discuss stopping and focusing on palliative care). Australian context: Home oxygen provided through Oxygen Therapy Program (requires respiratory physician prescription and assessment), PBS authority required for pirfenidone continuation (demonstrate FVC not declining >10% per year), lung transplant centres limited to Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane (long waiting times, 30-50% die waiting). Candidates should demonstrate compassionate communication about prognosis and goals of care.
osces.model_answer_summary: This 68-year-old man with IPF has progressive disease indicated by FVC decline from 68% to 52% predicted in 6 months (>10% absolute decline predicts increased mortality). Resting hypoxia (SpO2 88%) and severe exercise desaturation (78% on 6MWT) meet criteria for long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT). Immediate management: (1) Prescribe LTOT 2L/min continuous via nasal prongs (15+ hours/day) targeting SpO2 90-92%, increase to 4L/min during exertion, (2) Organize home oxygen concentrator + portable cylinders through Oxygen Therapy Program, (3) Continue pirfenidone 801mg TDS (slowing FVC decline from expected ~200mL/year to ~100mL/year, side effects: photosensitivity, GI upset - patient tolerating well), (4) Echocardiogram to assess pulmonary hypertension (clinical signs present: loud P2, elevated JVP, ankle oedema - RVSP likely >40mmHg), (5) Chest CT screen for lung cancer (7-fold increased risk, unexplained weight loss 8kg in 6 months concerning). Palliative care: (1) Early referral to palliative care team (evidence shows improved quality of life, reduced hospital admissions), (2) Dyspnoea management: morphine 2.5-5mg PO Q4H PRN (reduces central perception of breathlessness), lorazepam 0.5mg PRN (anxiety), (3) Advance care planning: discuss prognosis (median survival 3-5 years from diagnosis, rapid progression suggests <2 years remaining), resuscitation wishes (IPF patients have <1% survival post-CPR), preferred place of care (home vs hospital). Lung transplant: Age 68 borderline (traditional cutoff 65, some centres accept to 70), rapid FVC decline and low DLCO 38% meet criteria, discuss referral to St Vincent's Sydney transplant programme (waiting time 6-18 months, 30-50% die waiting, 5-year post-transplant survival 50-60%). Multidisciplinary follow-up: respiratory physician 4-weekly (monitor FVC, adjust oxygen), palliative care 2-weekly (symptom control), occupational therapy (mobility aids, energy conservation), pulmonary rehabilitation if tolerated (improves 6MWT distance and quality of life without changing lung function). Prognosis: poor given rapid progression, median survival now likely 12-24 months without transplant.
references: Raghu G, et al. An official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT clinical practice guideline: treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2015;192:e3-19
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) - Position statement on long-term oxygen therapy
Australian Oxygen Therapy Program - Home oxygen prescribing guidelines (SpO2 ≤88% criteria)
eTG Complete - Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis management with pirfenidone and nintedanib
King TE Jr, et al. A phase 3 trial of pirfenidone in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. N Engl J Med 2014;370:2083-92
PBS Schedule - Pirfenidone (Esbriet) 267mg capsules - Authority required for IPF (FVC 50-90% predicted)
Kreuter M, et al. Palliative care in interstitial lung disease: living well. Lancet Respir Med 2017;5:968-80

osces.title: Vocal Cord Dysfunction - Differentiation from Asthma

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Emergency Department
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute-onset shortness of breath and throat tightness. She describes difficulty getting air in (inspiratory difficulty). Multiple previous presentations to ED with similar episodes, each time treated as asthma with minimal improvement.
scenario.background: Diagnosed with 'asthma' 2 years ago after first episode of acute dyspnoea. Currently on salbutamol 100mcg PRN and beclomethasone 100mcg 2 puffs BD. Uses salbutamol up to 10 times daily with minimal relief. Episodes occur suddenly, often during exercise or stressful situations. No improvement with nebulized salbutamol in previous ED presentations. Works as high school teacher, finds episodes embarrassing in front of students. History of anxiety disorder managed with escitalopram 10mg daily. Non-smoker, no occupational exposures. No known allergies.
scenario.physical_examination: Young woman, appears anxious, audible inspiratory stridor. Respiratory examination: increased work of breathing with suprasternal and intercostal recession, inspiratory stridor loudest over trachea, symmetrical chest expansion, percussion resonant throughout, auscultation reveals harsh inspiratory sounds over trachea, clear breath sounds in lung fields with no wheeze. Cardiovascular examination normal. Peak expiratory flow 420 L/min (predicted 460 L/min - 91% predicted, normal). Flattened inspiratory loop on flow-volume loop when performed.

tasks: Obtain detailed history focusing on timing of symptoms (inspiration vs expiration), triggers, and response to asthma medications
Perform focused respiratory examination including auscultation over trachea to identify stridor
Differentiate vocal cord dysfunction from asthma based on clinical features (inspiratory difficulty, stridor, normal oxygen saturation, lack of response to bronchodilators)
Perform peak expiratory flow measurement and interpret normal result (excludes significant bronchospasm)
Review flow-volume loop demonstrating flattened inspiratory curve characteristic of extrathoracic airway obstruction
Assess for psychiatric comorbidities including anxiety and depression that commonly coexist with VCD
Explain diagnosis of vocal cord dysfunction to patient using clear, non-judgmental language
Demonstrate and teach rescue breathing techniques (pursed-lip breathing, panting breaths) to abort acute episodes
Arrange urgent ENT referral for direct laryngoscopy to visualize paradoxical vocal cord motion during episode
Refer to speech pathology for breathing retraining and vocal cord relaxation techniques
Optimize management of anxiety disorder and consider psychology referral for cognitive behavioural therapy
Taper and discontinue unnecessary asthma medications (no evidence of asthma)
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features distinguishing vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) from asthma: inspiratory difficulty, stridor, normal oxygen saturation, lack of response to bronchodilators
Understand pathophysiology of VCD: paradoxical adduction of vocal cords during inspiration causing functional airway obstruction
Interpret flow-volume loops showing flattened inspiratory curve (variable extrathoracic obstruction) vs flattened expiratory curve in asthma (intrathoracic obstruction)
Recognize common triggers for VCD: exercise, strong emotions, irritants (perfumes, cleaning products), gastro-oesophageal reflux
Understand association between VCD and psychiatric comorbidities: anxiety disorders in 40-50%, history of trauma or abuse in some cases
Apply diagnostic criteria for VCD: visualization of paradoxical vocal cord motion during episode (gold standard via flexible laryngoscopy)
Demonstrate rescue breathing techniques for acute VCD: pursed-lip breathing, panting breaths, focus on relaxing throat
Understand role of speech pathology in VCD management: breathing retraining exercises, laryngeal relaxation techniques (70-80% symptom improvement)
Recognize importance of multidisciplinary approach: respiratory medicine, ENT, speech pathology, psychology
Avoid overtreatment with asthma medications (oral corticosteroids, frequent bronchodilators) when VCD is primary diagnosis
marking_criteria: Elicits key historical features of VCD: difficulty getting air IN (inspiratory), sudden onset often with exercise or stress, throat tightness, lack of response to salbutamol, normal between episodes
Performs respiratory examination correctly identifying inspiratory stridor loudest over trachea (extrathoracic origin) rather than lung fields
Recognizes normal oxygen saturation (98% on room air) as inconsistent with severe asthma exacerbation
Performs and interprets peak expiratory flow: 420 L/min (91% predicted) is normal, excluding significant bronchospasm
Identifies flattened inspiratory curve on flow-volume loop as characteristic of variable extrathoracic obstruction (VCD pattern)
Assesses psychiatric history including anxiety disorder (40-50% comorbidity with VCD) and explores psychological triggers

Explains VCD diagnosis sensitively: 'Your symptoms are caused by your vocal cords closing when they should open during breathing in. This is not asthma, and it's not psychosomatic - it's a real physical problem that can be treated with breathing techniques.'

Demonstrates rescue breathing technique during consultation: 'When you feel an episode starting, try panting like a dog (demonstrate), or breathe through pursed lips slowly, focusing on relaxing your throat. This helps open the vocal cords.'
Arranges urgent ENT referral for flexible laryngoscopy during induced episode (exercise provocation if needed) to visualize paradoxical vocal cord adduction (diagnostic gold standard)
Refers to speech pathology within 1-2 weeks for breathing retraining exercises and laryngeal control techniques (evidence-based first-line treatment, 70-80% symptom improvement)
Reviews psychiatric medications and refers to psychologist for CBT addressing anxiety triggers (reduces VCD episode frequency)

Plans to wean asthma medications: 'Since this is VCD not asthma, we will gradually reduce your inhalers. Keep salbutamol for now in case you do have any asthma component, but we expect you won't need it once you learn the breathing techniques.'
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests ability to differentiate vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) from asthma, a common diagnostic challenge leading to inappropriate treatment and frequent ED presentations. Key assessment points: (1) Recognition of inspiratory difficulty (VCD) vs expiratory difficulty (asthma), (2) Normal oxygen saturation and peak flow despite apparent severe dyspnoea (excludes significant airway obstruction), (3) Flow-volume loop interpretation (flattened inspiratory curve in VCD vs flattened expiratory curve in asthma), (4) Awareness of psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety in 40-50% of VCD patients), (5) Non-pharmacological management approach (breathing techniques, speech pathology, psychology). Common errors: assuming all dyspnoea is asthma, continuing to escalate asthma treatment despite lack of response, missing psychiatric comorbidity, not referring to speech pathology (first-line treatment), using judgmental language ('it's all in your head') rather than validating symptoms. Australian context: Speech pathology services may require GP referral and have waiting times in rural areas (Young Hospital may not have on-site speech pathologist, consider telehealth from Wagga Wagga), ENT flexible laryngoscopy available at Young Hospital or Wagga Wagga Base Hospital, Medicare rebate for psychology sessions under Mental Health Treatment Plan (up to 10 sessions per year). Candidates should demonstrate empathetic communication recognizing patients often feel dismissed when told 'not asthma.'
osces.model_answer_summary: This 28-year-old woman has vocal cord dysfunction (VCD), not asthma, based on: (1) Inspiratory difficulty ('can't get air IN') and inspiratory stridor (asthma causes expiratory difficulty and wheeze), (2) Normal oxygen saturation 98% and normal peak flow 420 L/min during episode (excludes significant bronchospasm), (3) Lack of response to salbutamol across multiple presentations (VCD does not respond to bronchodilators), (4) Flow-volume loop showing flattened inspiratory curve (variable extrathoracic obstruction pattern characteristic of VCD). Pathophysiology: Paradoxical adduction of vocal cords during inspiration causes functional airway obstruction at laryngeal level. Triggers include exercise, stress, irritants. Immediate management: (1) Reassure patient during acute episode (anxiety worsens VCD), (2) Demonstrate rescue breathing techniques: pursed-lip breathing (breathe in through nose, out slowly through pursed lips) or panting breaths (rapid shallow breathing like a dog - prevents vocal cord closure), focus on relaxing throat muscles, (3) Sitting position with neck slightly flexed (opens airway). Diagnostic confirmation: Flexible laryngoscopy during provoked episode (exercise on treadmill or methacholine challenge) visualizes paradoxical vocal cord adduction during inspiration (diagnostic gold standard). Treatment plan: (1) Speech pathology referral (first-line treatment): breathing retraining, laryngeal control exercises, relaxation techniques - 70-80% symptom improvement over 4-8 weeks, (2) Psychology referral: CBT for anxiety management, identify and address psychological triggers, (3) Optimize GORD treatment if present (reflux can trigger VCD), (4) Wean asthma medications: discontinue beclomethasone (no evidence of asthma), keep salbutamol PRN initially (some patients have both VCD and asthma - coexists in 30-40%). Education: VCD is real physical problem, not 'psychosomatic' or 'panic attack', can be effectively managed with breathing techniques, episodes not life-threatening (reassuring as normal oxygen saturation maintained). Prognosis: Excellent with speech pathology intervention, 70-80% achieve significant symptom reduction, episodes become less frequent and less severe with breathing technique mastery. Follow-up: respiratory clinic 4-6 weeks (after speech pathology intervention), consider repeat flow-volume loop to document improvement.
references: Morris MJ, Christopher KL. Diagnostic criteria for the classification of vocal cord dysfunction. Chest 2010;138:1213-23
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) - Vocal cord dysfunction position statement
Dunn NM, et al. Vocal cord dysfunction: a review. Asthma Res Pract 2015;1:9
Christopher KL, et al. Vocal cord dysfunction presenting as asthma. N Engl J Med 1983;308:1566-70
Speech Pathology Australia - Clinical guideline for breathing pattern disorders including VCD
Sandage MJ, Zelazny SK. Paradoxical vocal fold motion: a tutorial on a complex disorder and the speech-language pathologist's role. Lang Speech Hear Serv Sch 2004;35:353-62

osces.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation - BiPAP Settings and Monitoring for COPD Exacerbation

scenario.setting: Young District Hospital Emergency Department
scenario.presenting_complaint: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD presents with worsening dyspnoea over 3 days. Treated with nebulized bronchodilators and oral corticosteroids but remains in respiratory distress. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg on 2L oxygen.
scenario.background: Known severe COPD (FEV1 32% predicted), previous ICU admission for NIV 12 months ago. Home oxygen therapy (2L continuous). Current medications: tiotropium 18mcg daily, salbutamol/ipratropium nebulizers QID, prednisolone 5mg daily, home oxygen 2L/min 16 hours/day. Ex-smoker (60 pack-year history, quit 2015). Lives alone in Young, usually independent with ADLs. Previous advance care directive completed: for non-invasive ventilation but not for intubation. No known allergies.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 88% on 2L via nasal prongs, 91% on 35% Venturi mask

scenario.physical_examination: Elderly man, severe respiratory distress, using accessory muscles, unable to speak full sentences. Mild confusion (GCS 14, E4 V4 M6). Respiratory examination: barrel chest, reduced chest expansion, hyperresonant percussion throughout, distant breath sounds with prolonged expiration, diffuse wheeze and scattered crackles. Cardiovascular: tachycardia, elevated JVP 8cm, mild bilateral ankle oedema. Asterixis present (CO2 retention). No peripheral cyanosis on supplemental oxygen.

tasks: Interpret arterial blood gas showing acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mmHg)
Recognize indications for non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in COPD: pH 7.25-7.35, hypercapnia, respiratory distress despite medical therapy
Apply NIV exclusion criteria and ensure patient suitable (conscious, cooperative, able to protect airway, no contraindications)
Initiate BiPAP with appropriate initial settings: IPAP 12-14 cmH2O, EPAP 4-5 cmH2O, FiO2 to target SpO2 88-92%
Select appropriate mask interface (oronasal vs nasal mask) and ensure proper fit to minimize leak
Monitor patient response to NIV: repeat ABG at 1-2 hours, assess respiratory rate, mental status, and patient comfort
Titrate BiPAP settings based on ABG and clinical response: increase IPAP to improve ventilation and reduce PaCO2, adjust EPAP to prevent atelectasis
Manage complications of NIV including mask leak, gastric distension, pressure ulcers, and patient intolerance
Continue medical therapy: bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics if infection suspected, and treat precipitating cause
Escalate to ICU if NIV failure criteria met: worsening acidosis pH <7.25, increasing PaCO2, decreased consciousness, or patient exhaustion
Document ceiling of care based on advance care directive (NIV acceptable, intubation declined)
Arrange HDU admission for NIV monitoring with 1:4 nursing ratio and respiratory support
learning_objectives: Interpret arterial blood gas distinguishing acute vs chronic respiratory acidosis (compare pH and PaCO2 to assess acuity)
Apply Australian guidelines for NIV in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (AHRF) in COPD exacerbation
Understand mechanism of BiPAP in COPD: IPAP supports inspiration (reduces work of breathing, improves ventilation), EPAP prevents alveolar collapse (improves oxygenation, recruits atelectatic areas)
Recognize NIV indications: pH 7.25-7.35, PaCO2 >45 mmHg with respiratory acidosis, respiratory rate >25, accessory muscle use despite medical therapy
Identify NIV contraindications: impaired consciousness (GCS <10), inability to protect airway, copious secretions, facial trauma, hemodynamic instability, pneumothorax
Demonstrate NIV initiation protocol: start with low pressures (IPAP 10-12, EPAP 4-5) and titrate up based on tolerance and ABG response
Monitor NIV effectiveness: clinical improvement (reduced respiratory rate, improved alertness), ABG improvement (rising pH, falling PaCO2) at 1-2 hours
Recognize NIV failure criteria requiring intubation: pH <7.25 despite NIV, worsening hypercapnia, decreasing consciousness, cardiovascular instability, patient exhaustion or intolerance
Understand importance of controlled oxygen therapy in COPD: target SpO2 88-92% to avoid hypercapnia from excessive oxygen (loss of hypoxic drive)
Coordinate care involving respiratory medicine, intensive care, nursing, physiotherapy, and palliative care if ceilings of care in place
marking_criteria: Correctly interprets ABG showing acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure: pH 7.28 (acidotic), PaCO2 68 mmHg (hypercapnia), PaO2 58 mmHg (hypoxia), likely elevated HCO3 (metabolic compensation from chronic CO2 retention - baseline PaCO2 probably 50-55 mmHg based on home oxygen requirement)
Recognizes pH 7.28 with PaCO2 68 mmHg and respiratory distress as clear indication for NIV (reduces intubation rate by 60%, reduces mortality by 40% in COPD exacerbations with respiratory acidosis)
Assesses NIV suitability: patient conscious (GCS 14), cooperative, able to protect airway (cough reflex present), no pneumothorax on CXR, hemodynamically stable - suitable for NIV

Initiates BiPAP with appropriate settings: IPAP 12 cmH2O (provides inspiratory support), EPAP 5 cmH2O (prevents alveolar collapse, intrinsic PEEP in COPD), FiO2 28-35% targeting SpO2 88-92% (avoid hyperoxia in COPD)
Selects oronasal mask (full face mask) for initial trial (better for mouth-breathers, more effective in acute setting compared to nasal mask)
Ensures proper mask fit: measure mask size (small/medium/large), apply with minimal strap tension initially (prevent pressure ulcers), check for air leak (excessive leak reduces efficacy)
Plans repeat ABG at 1-2 hours to assess NIV response: expect pH to rise toward 7.35, PaCO2 to fall by 5-10 mmHg, patient to appear more comfortable with reduced respiratory rate
Titrates BiPAP settings based on response: if pH not improving, increase IPAP by 2 cmH2O increments (maximum typically 20 cmH2O), maintain IPAP-EPAP gradient ≥8 cmH2O for effective ventilation

Monitors for NIV complications: gastric distension (common, use nasogastric tube if severe), pressure ulcers on nasal bridge (protective dressings, mask breaks every 2-4 hours), eye irritation from mask leak, claustrophobia (reassurance, anxiolytic if needed)

Continues medical therapy during NIV: salbutamol/ipratropium nebulizers 4-hourly, prednisolone 30-40mg daily for 5 days (or equivalent IV hydrocortisone if unable to take orally), amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg BD if purulent sputum suggests infection

Defines NIV failure criteria and escalation plan: if pH <7.25 at 2 hours, worsening PaCO2, decreased GCS, or patient exhaustion → assess for intubation BUT patient's advance directive states NOT for intubation → palliative care involvement, focus on comfort, consider palliative sedation if distressing dyspnoea

Arranges HDU admission (NIV requires close monitoring, 1:4 nursing ratio minimum, respiratory physiotherapy, medical oversight 1-2 hourly initially), documents ceiling of care (NIV acceptable, intubation declined), contacts family regarding serious condition and advance care directive
osces.examiner_notes: This OSCE tests competency in initiating and managing non-invasive ventilation (NIV) for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD exacerbation. Key assessment points: (1) Interpretation of ABG showing acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28 with PaCO2 68 suggests acute component as patient would be compensated if chronic), (2) Recognition of clear NIV indication based on evidence (reduces intubation and mortality in COPD with pH 7.25-7.35), (3) Appropriate BiPAP initial settings (start low, titrate up), (4) Understanding NIV monitoring and failure criteria (repeat ABG at 1-2 hours critical), (5) Respecting advance care directive (NIV yes, intubation no - important ethical and legal issue). Common errors: using nasal mask in acute setting (less effective), excessive oxygen therapy causing worsening hypercapnia (target SpO2 88-92% in COPD), starting IPAP too high (patient intolerance), not repeating ABG early enough to detect NIV failure, proceeding to intubation despite advance directive declining it. Australian context: NIV available in most rural hospitals HDU (Young Hospital has capability), BiPAP machines (Philips Respironics or ResMed commonly used), advance care directives legally binding in NSW (must be followed), ceiling of care discussions should involve patient/family/palliative care. Candidates should demonstrate clear communication about NIV purpose, realistic expectations (70-80% success rate in this scenario), and contingency planning if NIV fails given patient's wishes not for intubation.
osces.model_answer_summary: This 72-year-old man with severe COPD has acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure: pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg. Likely acute component (precipitant: infective exacerbation based on fever, increased sputum, crackles) superimposed on chronic CO2 retention (home oxygen requirement suggests baseline PaCO2 50-55 mmHg). Clear indication for BiPAP: pH 7.25-7.35 range, hypercapnia, respiratory distress despite medical therapy (reduces intubation by 60%, mortality by 40% in COPD exacerbations). NIV suitability: Patient conscious (GCS 14), cooperative, protecting airway, no contraindications (no pneumothorax, hemodynamically stable, no copious secretions). BiPAP settings: (1) Initial IPAP 12 cmH2O (supports inspiration, reduces work of breathing), EPAP 5 cmH2O (prevents alveolar collapse, overcomes intrinsic PEEP in COPD), (2) FiO2 28% targeting SpO2 88-92% (avoid hyperoxia - can worsen hypercapnia by reducing hypoxic drive and Haldane effect), (3) Oronasal mask (full face), size medium, apply with minimal strap tension. Monitoring: (1) Repeat ABG at 1 hour (expect pH rising toward 7.35, PaCO2 falling by 5-10 mmHg, PaO2 stable 60-70 mmHg on controlled oxygen), (2) Clinical parameters: respiratory rate (expect reduction to <25), mental status (improving alertness), patient comfort (tolerating mask), (3) Vital signs: HR, BP, SpO2 continuous monitoring. Titration: If 1-hour ABG shows inadequate improvement (pH <7.32), increase IPAP by 2 cmH2O to 14 cmH2O (repeat hourly until pH >7.32 or maximum IPAP 18-20 cmH2O reached). NIV failure criteria: pH <7.25 at 2 hours, worsening PaCO2, decreased GCS, cardiovascular instability, patient exhaustion → normally would intubate BUT patient has advance care directive declining intubation → palliative care involvement, focus on symptom control, consider morphine for refractory dyspnoea, discuss with family. Concurrent therapy: (1) Bronchodilators: salbutamol 5mg + ipratropium 500mcg nebulized 4-hourly, (2) Corticosteroids: prednisolone 40mg PO daily x 5 days, (3) Antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg BD x 5 days (fever and purulent sputum suggest bacterial infection), (4) Controlled oxygen: Venturi 28% (precise FiO2 delivery), (5) Physiotherapy: regular suctioning, cough assistance, chest physiotherapy when stable. Prognosis: 70-80% success rate with NIV in this scenario if started early, mortality 10-15% in-hospital if NIV successful, higher if NIV fails and intubation declined. HDU admission for close monitoring (1:2 or 1:4 nursing ratio, hourly observations, medical review 2-4 hourly).
references: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) - Guidelines for non-invasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure
Rochwerg B, et al. Official ERS/ATS clinical practice guidelines: noninvasive ventilation for acute respiratory failure. Eur Respir J 2017;50:1602426
British Thoracic Society/Intensive Care Society. Guidelines for the ventilatory management of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in adults. Thorax 2016;71:ii1-35
eTG Complete - Non-invasive ventilation in COPD exacerbation protocol
Davidson AC, et al. BTS/ICS guideline for the ventilatory management of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in adults. Thorax 2016;71:ii1-35 (adapted for Australian practice)
NSW Health - Advance care directive policy and legal framework

osces.title: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency - Diagnosis and Augmentation Therapy
osces.clinical_scenario: Mr O'Brien, a 42-year-old never-smoker, presents with a 3-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea. He was recently diagnosed with emphysema on CT chest performed for unrelated reasons. He reports his younger brother was diagnosed with 'liver problems' at age 35. He has noticed increasing breathlessness affecting his work performance and has had two chest infections in the past 6 months requiring antibiotics.

presenting_complaint.character: breathlessness on moderate exertion, walking one flight of stairs
presenting_complaint.exacerbating_factors: physical activity, cold air, dust exposure at work
presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: rest, salbutamol inhaler provides minimal relief
presenting_complaint.associated_symptoms: chronic dry cough, fatigue, no wheeze, no sputum production

medications: salbutamol MDI 100mcg PRN (PBS code 2178D)
recently started tiotropium 18mcg daily (PBS code 9086R)

social_history.alcohol: 5-10 standard drinks per week
social_history.occupation: warehouse supervisor, dust exposure, some heavy lifting
social_history.exercise: previously played social soccer, stopped due to breathlessness

history_taking.family_history: brother diagnosed with cirrhosis age 35 (non-drinker), maternal grandfather died of 'lung disease' age 58, parents of Irish descent

physical_examination.general: well-appearing man, mild dyspnoea at rest, no distress

respiratory.inspection: increased AP diameter, mild use of accessory muscles
respiratory.auscultation: globally reduced breath sounds, no wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase

physical_examination.cardiovascular: normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
physical_examination.abdomen: soft, non-tender, liver palpable 1cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly

initial.result: FEV1 1.95L (48% predicted), FVC 4.2L (82% predicted), FEV1/FVC 46%, post-bronchodilator FEV1 2.05L (51% predicted) - minimal reversibility, DLCO 45% predicted
0.42 g/L (normal 0.9-2.0 g/L)
PiZZ phenotype confirmed
ALT 68 U/L (normal <40), AST 52 U/L (normal <40), GGT 45 U/L, bilirubin 18 μmol/L, albumin 38 g/L
panlobular emphysema with basal predominance, no bronchiectasis, no nodules
pH 7.41, PaO2 68 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, SaO2 93%
hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace, paucity of vascular markings lower zones
mild hepatomegaly, increased echogenicity suggesting fatty infiltration, no cirrhosis

diagnosis.primary: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ phenotype) with emphysema
diagnosis.diagnostic_criteria: serum AAT level <0.5 g/L, PiZZ phenotype, panlobular emphysema with basal predominance in never-smoker

immediate: supplemental oxygen if SpO2 <88% on exertion
pulmonary function optimisation
smoking cessation counselling for household members
genetic counselling referral

pharmacological.pbs_code: not PBS listed - accessed via Life Saving Drugs Program
pharmacological.monitoring: trough AAT levels monthly initially, pulmonary function tests 6-monthly

non_pharmacological: avoid occupational dust exposure - consider work modification
family screening for siblings and children

osces.title: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis - Bird Fancier's Lung

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Westmead Hospital, Sydney
scenario.presentation: A 62-year-old retired librarian presents with 4 months of progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, and 5kg weight loss. She reports feeling breathless when climbing stairs and has noticed fevers in the evenings. Symptoms improve when she visits her daughter in Melbourne for a week but return upon coming home. She keeps 6 budgerigars in her living room and has done so for the past 18 months.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 91% on room air, 96% on 2L nasal prongs

scenario.past_medical_history: Hypertension (well-controlled on perindopril 5mg daily), osteoarthritis, no previous respiratory disease
